questions.question: A company runs a stateless web tier on EC2 instances in a single Availability Zone behind an Application Load Balancer. An AZ outage last quarter caused a full site outage. Which change MOST improves availability with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Take hourly AMIs of the instances, copy them to a second Region, and relaunch the web tier from the latest AMI with a runbook during an outage.
Replace the ALB with a Network Load Balancer with cross-zone load balancing enabled.
Configure the Auto Scaling group to span at least two Availability Zones and register it with the existing ALB, which is already multi-AZ.
Move the instances to a larger instance type with enhanced networking so the single AZ can absorb more load during incidents.
questions.explanation: Spreading the Auto Scaling group across multiple AZs behind an ALB removes the single-AZ failure domain and lets Auto Scaling replace capacity automatically. AMI copies to another Region are a DR measure with manual recovery, not HA. Switching to an NLB does not help if all targets are still in one AZ. A bigger instance does nothing for AZ failure.

questions.question: An application uses Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL in a single-AZ deployment. The business requires automatic failover within about a minute if the primary instance or its AZ fails, with no data loss. What should a solutions architect recommend?
options: Convert the instance to a Multi-AZ deployment so RDS maintains a synchronous standby and fails over automatically.
Create a cross-Region read replica and promote it to a standalone primary with a runbook when the primary instance fails.
Enable automated backups with a 35-day retention period and restore to a new instance on failure.
Create an in-Region read replica in another AZ and point the application at it using a Route 53 weighted record with health checks.
questions.explanation: Multi-AZ uses synchronous replication to a standby in another AZ and fails over automatically by flipping the DNS endpoint, giving near-zero RPO. Read replicas use asynchronous replication (possible data loss) and promotion is manual. Restoring from backups takes far longer than a minute. Weighted routing to a read-only replica would break writes.

questions.question: A financial services company runs Aurora PostgreSQL in us-east-1. Regulators require the ability to recover in a second Region with an RPO of about 1 second and RTO under 1 minute, while keeping the secondary Region able to serve local read traffic. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Configure cross-Region automated backup replication and restore the latest replicated snapshot into a new Aurora cluster in the DR Region during an event.
Use AWS DMS with ongoing CDC replication from the Aurora writer to an RDS for PostgreSQL Multi-AZ instance in the DR Region.
Create a cross-Region read replica of each Aurora instance using native PostgreSQL logical replication.
Use an Aurora Global Database with a secondary cluster in the DR Region and use managed switchover/failover to promote it during a Regional event.
questions.explanation: Aurora Global Database replicates storage-level changes with typical lag under 1 second and supports promoting the secondary in about a minute, while the secondary cluster serves reads. Snapshot restore gives RPO/RTO of hours. DMS CDC adds lag and operational overhead and a heterogeneous target. Hand-built logical replication is more fragile and not designed for sub-minute managed failover.

questions.question: A company stores critical documents in an S3 bucket in eu-west-1. It must keep a copy in another Region in case of a Regional outage, and also protect against accidental overwrites. What is the SIMPLEST approach?
options: Enable S3 Versioning on both buckets and configure S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) to a bucket in another Region.
Schedule a daily AWS DataSync task that copies all objects between the two buckets and verifies checksums after each run.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the source bucket so uploads are routed through edge locations in other Regions.
Configure an S3 Lifecycle rule to transition objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
questions.explanation: CRR asynchronously copies new objects to a bucket in another Region and requires versioning, which also preserves prior versions after overwrites. DataSync on a schedule works but adds operational overhead and a larger RPO. Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads over long distances; it does not replicate. Lifecycle transitions change storage class in the same Region and provide no Regional redundancy.

questions.question: An order-processing system has a web tier that sends orders directly to a backend service. During flash sales, the backend is overwhelmed and orders are lost. What design change MOST improves resiliency?
options: Increase the backend instance size so it has enough CPU and memory headroom to handle the flash-sale peak directly without any buffering.
Use Amazon SNS to publish each order directly to the backend HTTP endpoint and rely on SNS delivery retries.
Add an Amazon ElastiCache cluster in front of the backend.
Place an Amazon SQS queue between the tiers so the web tier enqueues orders and backend workers consume at their own pace.
questions.explanation: SQS decouples producers from consumers and durably buffers messages so spikes are absorbed and nothing is lost; workers can also scale on queue depth. Vertical scaling still has a ceiling and single-point characteristics. SNS push to HTTP retries but does not buffer indefinitely; if the backend is down, messages eventually fail. A cache does not help write-heavy order submission.

questions.question: A Lambda function processes messages from an SQS standard queue. Some messages contain malformed data and fail repeatedly, blocking processing capacity. What should be configured?
options: Increase the Lambda function timeout to 15 minutes so it has more time to process each difficult message.
Switch the queue to a FIFO queue so messages are processed strictly in order within each message group.
A dead-letter queue on the source SQS queue with an appropriate maxReceiveCount redrive policy.
Set the SQS message retention period to 14 days.
questions.explanation: A redrive policy moves messages that exceed maxReceiveCount to a DLQ for later inspection, so poison messages stop consuming retries. A longer timeout does not fix malformed input. FIFO queues would make it worse because a failing message blocks its message group. Longer retention only keeps poison messages around longer.

questions.question: A global payments company needs a relational, PostgreSQL-compatible database that accepts strongly consistent writes in two Regions simultaneously, with zero infrastructure management and 99.999% multi-Region availability. Which service fits BEST?
options: Amazon Aurora DSQL with a multi-Region cluster (two peered Regions plus a witness Region).
Aurora Global Database with write forwarding enabled on the secondary cluster so both Regions accept writes.
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Multi-AZ DB cluster with two readable standbys spread across Availability Zones.
Amazon DynamoDB global tables with eventual consistency.
questions.explanation: Aurora DSQL is serverless, PostgreSQL-compatible, and supports active-active multi-Region with strong consistency, designed for 99.999% multi-Region availability; a witness Region participates in quorum. Global Database has a single writer Region (write forwarding still routes writes to the primary). RDS Multi-AZ DB clusters are single-Region. DynamoDB is not relational and default global tables are eventually consistent.

questions.question: A gaming company uses DynamoDB global tables across three Regions. A new leaderboard feature requires that a read in any Region always returns the latest committed write, even during a Regional failure. What should the architect configure?
options: Keep the default multi-Region eventual consistency and use strongly consistent reads in each Region.
Enable DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) clusters in every Region so reads are served from a consistent in-memory cache.
Use DynamoDB Streams with a Lambda function that synchronously copies each write to the tables in every other Region.
Create the global table with multi-Region strong consistency (MRSC) across exactly three Regions (or two replicas plus a witness) and use strongly consistent reads.
questions.explanation: MRSC (GA June 2025) synchronously replicates writes to at least one other Region before acknowledging, so strongly consistent reads in any replica return the latest version; it requires exactly three Regions, optionally with a witness. Default global tables are eventually consistent across Regions—strong reads are only Region-local. DAX is an eventually consistent cache. Streams plus Lambda is asynchronous.

questions.question: A company needs a disaster recovery strategy for a line-of-business application with an RTO of 24 hours and RPO of 24 hours. Cost must be minimized. Which strategy is MOST appropriate?
options: Pilot light: keep a continuously replicating database and minimal core infrastructure running in the DR Region.
Backup and restore: take daily backups with AWS Backup, copy them to the DR Region, and restore infrastructure with IaC when needed.
Warm standby: run a scaled-down but fully functional copy of the whole stack in the DR Region at all times.
Multi-site active/active: serve production traffic from full-capacity deployments in two Regions simultaneously with DynamoDB global tables.
questions.explanation: With RTO/RPO measured in hours to a day, backup and restore is the cheapest option and is sufficient. Pilot light, warm standby, and active/active progressively reduce RTO/RPO but cost more because resources run continuously in the DR Region.

questions.question: A company wants a DR design where the core database is always replicated to the DR Region but application servers are only launched during a disaster. RTO is tens of minutes. Which DR strategy is this?
options: Backup and restore
Warm standby
Pilot light
Multi-site active/active
questions.explanation: Pilot light keeps the critical data layer live (replicating) and provisions the rest on failover, giving RTO in tens of minutes. Backup and restore replicates nothing live. Warm standby runs a scaled-down but fully functional copy of the whole stack. Active/active serves production traffic in both Regions.

questions.question: A retailer runs its checkout in us-west-2 with a scaled-down but fully functional copy in us-east-1 that receives no production traffic. During a Regional event, operators must shift traffic reliably even if the us-west-2 control plane is impaired. Which approach is MOST resilient?
options: Edit the Route 53 failover records in the console during the event, pointing them at the us-east-1 load balancers.
Update a CloudFormation stack in us-west-2 that changes the DNS configuration and scales the us-east-1 fleet.
Rely on a Lambda function in us-west-2 that updates DNS when a CloudWatch alarm fires.
Use Amazon Route 53 Application Recovery Controller routing controls (data-plane) to flip failover DNS records, and scale up the us-east-1 Auto Scaling groups.
questions.explanation: Route 53 ARC routing controls are designed to be operated through a highly available data plane, avoiding dependence on control-plane APIs during an event; this is a warm standby failover. Console edits and CloudFormation depend on control planes that may be impaired. A Lambda in the failing Region may not run at all.

questions.question: An application writes session state to the local disk of EC2 instances. When Auto Scaling terminates an instance, users are logged out. What is the BEST fix?
options: Enable sticky sessions on the ALB with a long cookie duration and disable scale-in so instances are never terminated.
Attach a larger EBS volume to each instance so session files are retained across application restarts.
Use an EC2 placement group so instances are close together.
Store session state externally in Amazon ElastiCache (for example Valkey) or DynamoDB so instances become stateless.
questions.explanation: Externalizing session state makes the web tier stateless so any instance can serve any user and scale-in is safe. Sticky sessions plus disabling scale-in loses elasticity and still fails on instance failure. EBS volume size and placement groups do not address state loss when instances terminate.

questions.question: A company has a shared file system used by Linux EC2 instances in three AZs. The file system must survive an AZ failure and scale automatically. Which storage is MOST appropriate?
options: An EBS io2 Block Express volume with Multi-Attach enabled and attached to every instance in the three AZs.
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server with a single-AZ deployment and daily automatic backups.
Amazon EFS with the Regional (multi-AZ) file system type and a mount target in each AZ.
An S3 bucket mounted with a FUSE driver on each instance to present objects as a shared directory.
questions.explanation: EFS Regional file systems store data redundantly across multiple AZs, grow elastically, and are mountable over NFS from each AZ. EBS Multi-Attach works only within a single AZ and requires a cluster-aware file system. FSx for Windows single-AZ uses SMB and does not survive AZ failure. FUSE-mounted S3 lacks POSIX semantics and is not a true shared file system.

questions.question: A team needs to be notified and automatically recover an EC2 instance when the underlying host has a hardware failure. The instance is not in an Auto Scaling group. What is the simplest solution?
options: Create a Lambda function that polls the instance status every minute through the EC2 API and reboots the instance when a check fails.
Enable detailed monitoring on the instance so hardware failures are detected within one minute.
Take hourly EBS snapshots and restore manually.
Rely on EC2 simplified automatic recovery (enabled by default on supported instances) or create a CloudWatch alarm on StatusCheckFailed_System with the recover action.
questions.explanation: EC2 automatic recovery migrates the instance to healthy hardware keeping instance ID, private IPs, and EBS volumes; a CloudWatch alarm with the recover action achieves the same explicitly. Polling Lambda adds custom code and rebooting does not move hosts. Detailed monitoring only increases metric frequency. Snapshots are a backup, not recovery automation.

questions.question: A company has 200 AWS accounts. Compliance requires daily backups of all RDS, DynamoDB, and EBS resources tagged backup=true, with copies in a separate account that even the workload account root users cannot delete. Which solution meets this?
options: Use AWS Backup with an organization-wide backup policy from AWS Organizations, cross-account copy to a central backup account, and AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode (or a logically air-gapped vault).
Have each account run a scheduled Lambda function that creates snapshots of tagged resources and shares them with a central account.
Enable RDS automated backups with 35-day retention and DynamoDB PITR in each workload account.
Use AWS Config rules to detect untagged resources and alert.
questions.explanation: Organization backup policies centrally enforce tag-based plans across accounts; cross-account copies isolate backups and Vault Lock compliance mode (WORM) prevents deletion by anyone, including root. Custom Lambda scripting is high overhead and not immutable. Native service backups stay in the same account and can be deleted. Config only detects; it does not back up.

questions.question: An API built on API Gateway and Lambda experiences occasional throttling errors from a downstream third-party API. What pattern should the Lambda code use to improve resilience?
options: Retry immediately in a tight loop until the third-party API succeeds, so no request is dropped.
Increase the Lambda memory to 10,240 MB so the function gets more CPU and network bandwidth.
Switch the API Gateway endpoint from Regional to edge-optimized to spread calls across locations.
Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, with a bounded number of attempts.
questions.explanation: Exponential backoff with jitter spreads retries and avoids retry storms, the AWS-recommended approach for throttling. Tight retries amplify load. More memory does not affect third-party throttling. Endpoint type only changes client routing.

questions.question: A company wants its public web application to fail over to a static maintenance page hosted in S3 when the primary ALB becomes unhealthy. Which Route 53 configuration achieves this?
options: A weighted routing policy with a weight of 100 for the ALB and 0 for the S3 website endpoint, with no health checks.
A failover routing policy with the ALB as primary (with health evaluation) and the S3 static website as secondary.
A geolocation routing policy with a default location record that points to the S3 website.
A simple routing policy containing both the ALB and S3 website values in one record set.
questions.explanation: Failover routing returns the secondary only when the primary health check fails. Weighted with weight 0 would not automatically fail over unless all nonzero records are unhealthy and configured carefully; it is not the intended pattern. Geolocation routes by user location. Simple routing returns values randomly and has no health checks.

questions.question: A containerized microservice on ECS Fargate must remain available during an AZ impairment where instances are reachable but degraded (gray failure). Which approach helps the service shift away from the impaired AZ quickly?
options: Disable cross-zone load balancing on the ALB so that each AZ only receives traffic from clients in the same AZ.
Enable ALB zonal shift / zonal autoshift through Amazon Application Recovery Controller and run tasks in at least three AZs with capacity headroom.
Pin all tasks to the single AZ that has the most capacity and use placement constraints to keep them there.
Use an ECS capacity provider strategy with Fargate Spot only so tasks are rescheduled automatically into other AZs when they are interrupted.
questions.explanation: Zonal shift moves load balancer traffic away from an impaired AZ, and autoshift can do it automatically; static stability (pre-provisioned headroom across 3 AZs) ensures remaining AZs can absorb traffic. Disabling cross-zone does not remove an AZ. Single-AZ is the opposite of resilient. Fargate Spot lowers cost but adds interruption risk.

questions.question: Which statement about S3 storage class durability and availability is correct for S3 One Zone-IA?
options: It replicates data synchronously across three AZs, exactly like S3 Standard-IA, but at a lower price because it has fewer features.
It is designed for 99.99% availability, the same as S3 Standard, because it uses the same hardware.
It automatically fails over objects to another AZ in the Region if its primary AZ has an outage.
It offers 11 nines of durability within a single AZ but data is lost if that AZ is destroyed, so it suits re-creatable data.
questions.explanation: One Zone-IA stores data in one AZ (designed for 99.5% availability) and is appropriate for secondary copies or re-creatable data. It does not replicate across AZs, has lower availability than Standard (99.99%), and has no automatic failover.

questions.question: A company needs to run a batch analytics job nightly. The job can be interrupted and restarted from checkpoints. Which EC2 purchasing option provides the lowest cost while remaining resilient to interruptions?
options: On-Demand Instances in a single AZ, which cannot be interrupted and can be stopped when the job ends.
Spot Instances across multiple instance types and AZs using a diversified allocation strategy (for example price-capacity-optimized).
Dedicated Hosts purchased with a 1-year reservation so that capacity is always available and never interrupted during the nightly batch window.
A single Spot instance type in a single AZ with the lowest current price, relaunched when interrupted.
questions.explanation: Diversifying Spot across types and AZs with price-capacity-optimized lowers interruption likelihood and cost, and checkpointing handles interruptions. On-Demand and Dedicated Hosts cost more. A single type/AZ increases the chance of capacity loss.

questions.question: An e-commerce company uses a Step Functions workflow to orchestrate payment, inventory, and shipping microservices. If shipping fails, payment must be refunded. Which pattern should be implemented?
options: A two-phase commit coordinated across all of the microservice databases before any step is confirmed.
The saga pattern with compensating transactions implemented as Catch/fallback states in Step Functions.
A single Lambda function that calls the payment, inventory, and shipping services synchronously in sequence.
An SNS topic fan-out so that each microservice processes the order independently and in parallel.
questions.explanation: Sagas coordinate distributed transactions with compensating actions (refund on failure); Step Functions Catch and Retry make this explicit and observable. Two-phase commit across independent services is not practical. One monolithic Lambda loses durability and hits timeouts. SNS fan-out has no coordination or compensation.

questions.question: A web application on EC2 must scale out before CPU saturates during a predictable morning traffic surge every weekday. What is the MOST effective scaling approach?
options: Use predictive scaling (or a scheduled action) combined with target tracking on the Auto Scaling group.
Use a simple scaling policy triggered by a CloudWatch alarm on 5-minute average CPU utilization above 70%.
Manually increase the desired capacity of the Auto Scaling group each weekday morning before the surge.
Use step scaling policies triggered by an alarm on the ALB HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count metric.
questions.explanation: Predictive scaling forecasts recurring patterns and launches capacity in advance; target tracking handles unexpected deviations. Simple scaling reacts late with cooldowns. Manual scaling is error-prone. Scaling on 5XX errors reacts only after users are impacted.

questions.question: An application uses DynamoDB. The team needs to recover from accidental table writes that happened at an unknown time within the last two weeks. Which feature should be enabled?
options: DynamoDB Streams with a 24-hour retention, replaying the stored change records in reverse order to undo the accidental writes.
Point-in-time recovery (PITR), which allows restore to any second within the configured recovery period (up to 35 days).
On-demand capacity mode, which keeps every version of each item available for automatic rollback.
Global tables with a replica in a second Region that can be used to recover the previous item values.
questions.explanation: PITR provides continuous backups and restores to any point in the recovery window (configurable 1–35 days). Streams retain only 24 hours and are not a backup. Capacity mode is unrelated. Global tables replicate the bad writes too.

questions.question: A company runs a self-managed Kafka cluster on EC2 that frequently loses brokers during patching. They want a managed, highly available, Kafka-compatible option without managing broker capacity. Which is BEST?
options: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams in provisioned mode with enhanced fan-out consumers for each application.
Amazon MQ for RabbitMQ in a three-node cluster deployment across multiple Availability Zones.
Amazon MSK Serverless (or MSK Express brokers) deployed across three AZs.
Amazon SQS FIFO queues.
questions.explanation: MSK is Kafka-compatible and handles broker replacement and patching across AZs; Serverless removes capacity planning. Kinesis would require rewriting producers/consumers. Amazon MQ RabbitMQ is not Kafka. SQS FIFO is a queue, not a Kafka log with consumer groups and replay.

questions.question: A solutions architect must design a highly available NAT solution for private subnets in three AZs. Which design follows best practice?
options: Deploy a single zonal NAT gateway in one AZ for all private subnets.
Run a NAT instance in an Auto Scaling group of one with a script that updates route tables on replacement.
Attach an internet gateway directly to the private subnets and remove public IPs from the instances.
Use a NAT gateway in regional availability mode (which expands across AZs automatically), or one zonal NAT gateway per AZ with each private subnet routed to its own AZ gateway.
questions.explanation: Zonal NAT gateways are AZ-scoped, so the classic pattern is one per AZ with AZ-local routes; since November 2025 a regional NAT gateway automatically expands and contracts across AZs where workloads run, without needing public subnets. A single zonal NAT gateway is a single-AZ failure point with cross-AZ charges. NAT instances add management and failover delay. Routing private subnets to an IGW makes them public.

questions.question: A company needs a managed Microsoft SQL Server database that survives an AZ failure with automatic failover. Which option requires the LEAST effort?
options: SQL Server on EC2 with Always On availability groups configured manually.
Amazon RDS for SQL Server with Multi-AZ enabled.
RDS for SQL Server Single-AZ with daily snapshots.
Aurora PostgreSQL with Babelfish only.
questions.explanation: RDS Multi-AZ for SQL Server provides managed synchronous standby and automatic failover. EC2 with Always On works but is self-managed. Snapshots do not provide automatic failover. Babelfish may require app changes and is a migration, not the least-effort HA option.

questions.question: A SaaS provider must meet a 99.99% availability SLO for its API. A dependency analysis shows a single-Region DynamoDB table and Lambda are fine, but a third-party auth provider is a hard dependency with 99.9% availability. What is the BEST way to improve overall availability?
options: Add more Lambda reserved and provisioned concurrency so requests waiting on the auth provider do not queue up.
Move the DynamoDB table to a larger provisioned capacity with auto scaling to absorb retries.
Reduce the hard dependency: cache validated tokens/JWKS locally, validate tokens statelessly, and degrade gracefully when the provider is unavailable.
Deploy the API to a second Region while still calling the auth provider synchronously on every request.
questions.explanation: Serial hard dependencies multiply availability, so a 99.9% dependency caps the service below 99.99%. Stateless JWT validation with cached keys removes the per-request call. More concurrency or capacity does not affect the third party. A second Region still inherits the same hard dependency.

questions.question: An S3-hosted static website fronted by CloudFront must continue serving content if the primary S3 origin in one Region becomes unavailable. What should be configured?
options: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the origin bucket so CloudFront can fetch objects through other Regions.
Increase the CloudFront default and maximum TTL to one year so objects are rarely fetched from the origin.
Create a second CloudFront distribution in another Region.
A CloudFront origin group with a primary and secondary S3 origin (replicated with CRR) for origin failover.
questions.explanation: Origin groups fail over to a secondary origin on specified HTTP errors or timeouts. Transfer Acceleration is for uploads. Long TTLs help only for cached objects. CloudFront is global; a second distribution does not provide origin failover by itself.

questions.question: What does RPO represent in disaster recovery planning?
options: The maximum acceptable time between the start of an outage and the restoration of the service to users.
The percentage of time over a year during which a system is available and serving requests successfully.
The maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time since the last recovery point.
The number of Regions a workload runs in.
questions.explanation: Recovery Point Objective is about data loss (how far back you can go). Recovery Time Objective is downtime. Availability percentage and Region count are different metrics.

questions.question: A media company runs a long-running (up to several days) multi-step video pipeline that waits on human review approvals. They want to write it as ordinary code in Lambda, without paying for compute while waiting, and resume automatically after failures. Which option fits BEST?
options: AWS Lambda durable functions, using checkpointed steps and waits/callbacks that suspend execution for up to one year without compute charges.
A standard Lambda function with a 15-minute timeout that polls a DynamoDB table for the approval status.
An EC2 instance running a cron-based script that checks for approvals and resumes the pipeline steps.
Amazon SQS delay queues with the 15-minute maximum delay, re-enqueuing the message repeatedly from a consumer until the approval arrives.
questions.explanation: Lambda durable functions (re:Invent 2025) use checkpoint-and-replay so completed steps are skipped on retry, and waits suspend execution without charges for up to a year. Standard Lambda caps at 15 minutes. EC2 cron is always-on cost and self-managed. Chained delay queues are brittle. Step Functions Standard would also work, but the requirement is to write it as ordinary Lambda code.

questions.question: An application running in an Auto Scaling group registers instances with an ALB. Instances are marked healthy by EC2 status checks even when the application process has crashed. What should be changed?
options: Increase the health check grace period to 1 hour so instances have more time to recover the application process before being evaluated.
Switch to a Network Load Balancer, which performs TCP health checks on the application port.
Enable termination protection on the instances so Auto Scaling cannot remove them unexpectedly.
Enable ELB health checks on the Auto Scaling group so instances failing the ALB target health check are replaced.
questions.explanation: With ELB health checks, Auto Scaling uses the load balancer view (application-level) to replace unhealthy instances. A longer grace period delays detection. An NLB does not change ASG health check type. Termination protection keeps broken instances around.

questions.question: A company wants to validate that its multi-AZ architecture actually tolerates the loss of an AZ, and wants repeatable experiments with stop conditions tied to CloudWatch alarms. Which approach is BEST?
options: Run AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS) experiments, such as the AZ power interruption scenario, with CloudWatch alarm stop conditions.
Manually terminate instances in production during business hours and observe how the application behaves.
Review the architecture diagram against the Reliability pillar questions in the Well-Architected Tool.
Enable AWS Config rules for multi-AZ resources.
questions.explanation: FIS provides managed, repeatable chaos experiments including AZ-level scenarios and safety stop conditions. Manual termination is unsafe and unrepeatable. A WA review is useful but does not test behavior. Config checks configuration, not actual failure behavior.

questions.question: A company wants to protect a workload against a Region-wide failure of Amazon S3 in the primary Region while keeping a single global endpoint for reads and writes. Which feature helps?
options: S3 Object Lock in governance mode on the bucket so objects cannot be deleted during a Regional event.
S3 Intelligent-Tiering, which stores objects across multiple Regions to optimize availability and cost.
S3 Multi-Region Access Points with bidirectional replication and failover controls.
S3 Access Grants that map users to buckets in each Region through a single grants instance.
questions.explanation: Multi-Region Access Points provide one global endpoint routing to the closest healthy bucket, with active/passive failover controls and replication. Object Lock is WORM retention. Intelligent-Tiering is cost optimization. Access Grants manage permissions.

questions.question: An ECS service must maintain at least 6 running tasks during deployments while replacing all tasks with a new version. Which setting controls this?
options: Set the task definition CPU and memory to the maximum values so each task can absorb more traffic.
Use a Network Load Balancer instead of an ALB so connections are drained faster and tasks are replaced in parallel during deployments.
Enable ECS Exec on the service so operators can keep tasks running while the new version starts.
Set minimumHealthyPercent (for example 100%) and maximumPercent (for example 200%) in the service deployment configuration.
questions.explanation: Rolling deployments use minimumHealthyPercent and maximumPercent to bound the number of tasks during replacement. CPU sizing, load balancer type, and ECS Exec do not control deployment capacity.

questions.question: An enterprise runs a mission-critical application across two Regions in active/active mode using DynamoDB global tables and Route 53 latency routing. During a partial failure, both Regions accept writes to the same item. What conflict resolution behavior should the architect expect with default (eventually consistent) global tables?
options: Last writer wins based on timestamps, so the application must be designed to tolerate or avoid concurrent cross-Region writes to the same item.
DynamoDB detects the conflict and rejects the second write with a ConditionalCheckFailedException error.
Both writes are merged attribute by attribute automatically, keeping the newest value of each field.
Writes are queued and then applied in the order determined by the designated primary Region.
questions.explanation: Default global tables use last-writer-wins reconciliation; designs often route writes for a given key to a home Region or use MRSC when strong consistency is required. DynamoDB does not reject cross-Region conflicts or merge attributes, and there is no primary Region in multi-active global tables.

questions.question: An application running on a single EC2 instance uses an Elastic IP. The team wants to reduce downtime from instance failure without redesigning the app. What is a quick improvement?
options: Purchase a Reserved Instance for the instance so capacity is reserved for it in its Availability Zone.
Enable hibernation so the instance can resume quickly with its in-memory state after a failure.
Place the instance in an Auto Scaling group with min=max=1 across multiple AZs, bootstrapping from an AMI/launch template and reattaching configuration on launch.
Use an instance store volume for the root disk so the instance boots faster after a failure.
questions.explanation: An ASG of one self-heals by replacing a failed instance in any configured AZ. Reserved Instances are a billing construct. Hibernation does not help failure. Instance store is ephemeral and makes recovery worse.

questions.question: Which ELB type should be used when clients require static IP addresses per AZ and the protocol is TCP/UDP at very high throughput?
options: Network Load Balancer
Application Load Balancer
Classic Load Balancer
Gateway Load Balancer
questions.explanation: NLB operates at layer 4, supports TCP/UDP/TLS, handles millions of requests per second, and provides one static IP (or Elastic IP) per AZ. ALB is layer 7 without static IPs. CLB is legacy. GWLB is for inserting third-party virtual appliances.

questions.question: A regulated company must ensure backups cannot be deleted or altered for 7 years, even by administrators, and wants the ability to recover even if its entire AWS Organization management account is compromised. What should they use?
options: S3 Versioning with MFA Delete enabled on a backup bucket in the same account, protected by the root user MFA device held by the security team.
EBS snapshots protected by a tag-based IAM policy that denies ec2:DeleteSnapshot for all administrators.
AWS Backup logically air-gapped vault (or Vault Lock in compliance mode) with retention of 7 years, shared to a recovery account.
AWS Config conformance packs that continuously check backup plans and report deletions.
questions.explanation: Logically air-gapped vaults are locked in compliance mode, encrypted with AWS-owned keys, and can be shared via RAM to a separate account for recovery—designed for ransomware and account-compromise scenarios. MFA Delete and IAM denies can be bypassed by privileged admins. Config does not create backups.

questions.question: A team deploys a Lambda function that must not be throttled by other functions in the account during peak events. What should be configured?
options: A larger memory setting.
A provisioned throughput setting on API Gateway.
Reserved concurrency for the function.
An SQS FIFO queue in front of the function.
questions.explanation: Reserved concurrency guarantees a portion of the account concurrency pool to the function (and caps it). Memory affects CPU/performance, not concurrency guarantees. API Gateway throttling limits clients. FIFO queues do not reserve Lambda concurrency.

questions.question: A solutions architect is designing for resilience. Which Well-Architected Reliability design principle is demonstrated by using Auto Scaling to replace failed instances automatically?
options: Automatically recover from failure.
Stop guessing capacity by monitoring demand and scaling.
Manage change through automation with infrastructure as code.
Test recovery procedures regularly in a staging environment.
questions.explanation: Replacing failed instances automatically based on health is the principle "automatically recover from failure". The others are also reliability principles but describe different practices (scaling to demand, IaC-driven change, and testing).

questions.question: A company runs an SAP HANA workload on EC2 and wants cross-Region DR with block-level replication, RPO of seconds and RTO of minutes, without maintaining standby compute. Which AWS service is designed for this?
options: AWS DataSync tasks scheduled every 5 minutes to copy the database files to the DR Region.
AWS Backup daily EBS snapshots of the HANA volumes copied automatically to the DR Region.
Amazon S3 Cross-Region Replication of frequent database exports written to a bucket in the primary Region.
AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery, replicating to a low-cost staging area in the DR Region and launching recovery instances on demand.
questions.explanation: Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS) performs continuous block-level replication (RPO seconds) and launches recovery instances in minutes, paying only for staging storage until failover. DataSync is file/object transfer. Daily snapshots give RPO of a day. Exports via S3 do not give seconds RPO.

questions.question: An application uses Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey as a cache. The team wants the cache to survive a node or AZ failure with automatic promotion of a replica. What should they enable?
options: Cluster/replication group with replicas in multiple AZs and Multi-AZ with automatic failover enabled (or use ElastiCache Serverless).
A single-node cluster with automatic daily backups that can be restored to a new node in another AZ after a node or AZ failure.
Memcached with auto discovery so clients reconnect to healthy nodes after a failure.
Data tiering on r6gd nodes so data is stored on local SSDs that survive node failures.
questions.explanation: Multi-AZ with automatic failover promotes a replica in another AZ; ElastiCache Serverless is multi-AZ by default. A single node is a single point of failure. Memcached has no replication. Data tiering is a cost/capacity feature.

questions.question: An organization wants a durable primary database for a microservice that needs Redis-compatible APIs with microsecond reads and multi-AZ durability for writes (no data loss on node failure). Which service fits?
options: Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached
Amazon MemoryDB
Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
Amazon RDS for MySQL
questions.explanation: MemoryDB is a durable, Redis/Valkey-compatible in-memory database with a multi-AZ transaction log. Memcached is a volatile cache without replication. DAX is a DynamoDB-only cache. RDS MySQL is not Redis-compatible.

questions.question: A company uses a hub account with an EventBridge bus to route events from 50 workload accounts. If the target Lambda in the hub is throttled or down, events must not be lost. What should be configured?
options: Increase the Lambda timeout and memory so the hub function can process each event before throttling occurs and retries are never needed.
Use EventBridge Scheduler instead of rules so events are delivered on a fixed schedule to the Lambda.
Configure EventBridge rule targets with a retry policy and a dead-letter queue (SQS), and consider archive and replay on the event bus.
Enable CloudTrail data events for EventBridge so failed deliveries can be replayed from the trail.
questions.explanation: EventBridge retries delivery for up to 24 hours (configurable) and can send failed events to a DLQ; archives allow replay. Timeout changes do not help throttling. Scheduler is for scheduled invocations. CloudTrail records API activity, not event recovery.

questions.question: A web application needs to handle a sudden 10x traffic increase for static images without scaling the origin EC2 fleet. What should be used?
options: A larger EC2 instance type with enhanced networking to serve more concurrent image requests.
AWS Global Accelerator in front of the ALB to route users over the AWS global network to the web tier.
Amazon CloudFront with appropriate cache behaviors for the static content (optionally S3 as origin).
An additional NAT gateway in each AZ to increase outbound bandwidth from the web tier.
questions.explanation: CloudFront caches static content at edge locations, offloading origin requests. Bigger instances still hit origin limits. Global Accelerator improves routing but does not cache. NAT gateways are for outbound traffic from private subnets.

questions.question: Which SQS feature ensures messages are processed exactly once and in order within a message group?
options: SQS standard queues with long polling enabled to reduce empty and duplicate receives.
SQS delay queues that hold each message for a fixed interval before delivery.
SQS FIFO queues with message deduplication and message group IDs.
SQS visibility timeout set to 12 hours.
questions.explanation: FIFO queues guarantee ordering per message group and exactly-once processing within a 5-minute deduplication interval. Standard queues provide at-least-once, best-effort ordering. Delay and visibility settings do not provide ordering.

questions.question: A company runs EKS clusters and wants nodes, load balancers, storage, and networking managed by AWS, with automatic node patching and right-sizing, to reduce operational toil while maintaining multi-AZ resilience. Which option fits BEST?
options: Self-managed node groups with Cluster Autoscaler.
EKS on Fargate for all workloads including DaemonSets.
Amazon ECS with EC2 launch type.
Amazon EKS Auto Mode.
questions.explanation: EKS Auto Mode manages compute autoscaling, pod networking, load balancing, block storage, and node lifecycle/patching as core components. Self-managed node groups are the most toil. Fargate does not support DaemonSets. ECS would require migrating off Kubernetes.

questions.question: An application needs to process uploaded files as soon as they land in S3, reliably, even if the processor is temporarily unavailable. Which design is MOST resilient?
options: S3 event notification directly invoking the Lambda function asynchronously, with no DLQ or on-failure destination.
A cron job on EC2 that lists the bucket every hour and processes any new objects it finds.
S3 event notification to an SQS queue, with Lambda (or workers) consuming from the queue and a DLQ.
S3 Inventory reports generated daily and processed by a batch job to find new uploads.
questions.explanation: Buffering events in SQS provides durability, retries, and a DLQ for failures. Direct async Lambda invocation retries only twice by default and without a destination events can be dropped. Hourly listing and inventory reports add latency and cost.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of deploying an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster (one writer, two readable standbys) compared with a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment?
options: It replicates data to readable standbys in other Regions automatically for disaster recovery.
It removes the need for automated backups because each standby holds a full copy of the data.
Faster failover (typically under 35 seconds) and the standbys can serve read traffic.
It supports an unlimited number of read replicas that share the same cluster storage volume.
questions.explanation: Multi-AZ DB clusters use semi-synchronous replication to two readable standbys in different AZs, giving faster failovers and read scaling. They are single-Region, still need backups, and have two standbys, not unlimited replicas.

questions.question: A company has a strict requirement that its disaster recovery Region must be able to operate even if it cannot reach any control-plane APIs in the primary Region. Which principle should guide the design?
options: Use CloudFormation StackSets in the primary Region to deploy DR resources at failover time.
Static stability: pre-provision capacity and configuration in the DR Region and depend only on data-plane operations to fail over.
Rely on Auto Scaling in the DR Region to launch all capacity on failover.
Use a single IAM Identity Center instance in the primary Region with no break-glass access.
questions.explanation: Static stability means the system keeps working without making changes during the event; data-plane operations are more available than control-plane operations. Launching everything via control planes at failover time, or depending on primary-Region services, violates this. Also plan break-glass access in case identity services are impaired.

questions.question: A team is running a stateful application on a single EBS volume. What is the recommended way to protect the data against volume failure and enable point-in-time recovery?
options: Enable EBS encryption with a customer managed KMS key so the data is protected on the volume.
Use RAID 0 across two volumes so the data is striped and can survive the loss of one volume.
Switch to an instance store volume, which is physically attached to the host for better durability.
Schedule EBS snapshots with Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager or AWS Backup.
questions.explanation: Snapshots are incremental, stored in S3-backed infrastructure, and allow recovery to a point in time; DLM/AWS Backup automates them. Encryption protects confidentiality. RAID 0 increases failure probability. Instance store is ephemeral.

questions.question: An application sends notifications to multiple downstream systems (email service, analytics, auditing). Each must receive every message and process independently even if one is down. What is the BEST pattern?
options: A single SQS queue shared by all consumers, each polling the same queue for new messages.
SNS topic fan-out to multiple SQS queues, one per downstream consumer.
Direct HTTP calls from the producer to each consumer, with retries implemented in the producer.
A DynamoDB table that the producer writes to and that each consumer polls for new items.
questions.explanation: SNS-to-SQS fan-out delivers a copy to each queue so consumers are isolated and can be down without losing messages. A shared queue delivers each message to only one consumer. Direct calls couple the producer to all consumers. Polling a table is inefficient.

questions.question: An IoT platform ingests 200 MB/s of telemetry into Kinesis Data Streams. Occasionally a record is up to 5 MiB (firmware diagnostics). Previously they stored these in S3 and sent pointers. What is the SIMPLEST current approach?
options: Split each large record into 1 MiB chunks and reassemble in consumers.
Move the whole telemetry pipeline to Amazon SQS standard queues with the Extended Client Library.
Switch to Amazon MSK Serverless and rewrite the producers and consumers to use Kafka clients.
Increase the stream maximum record size (up to 10 MiB) with UpdateMaxRecordSize and send the intermittent large records directly.
questions.explanation: Since October 2025, Kinesis Data Streams supports records up to 10 MiB (default remains 1 MiB, configurable per stream) for intermittent large payloads alongside normal traffic. Chunking adds complexity. SQS is 1 MiB max and not a stream. MSK is a heavier migration.

questions.question: A company wants to be alerted if a scheduled nightly batch job does not run at all. Which CloudWatch alarm setting helps detect this?
options: Set the alarm period to 10 seconds using high-resolution metrics so a missed run is noticed immediately.
Treat missing data as notBreaching so the alarm stays in OK state until the job reports a failure.
Configure the alarm to treat missing data as breaching on a metric the job emits each run.
Use a composite alarm with no child alarms so it evaluates the job schedule automatically.
questions.explanation: Treating missing data as breaching alerts when the expected datapoint is absent. High-resolution periods do not help. notBreaching hides the failure. A composite alarm needs child alarms.

questions.question: Which AWS service provides a managed way to run the same CloudFormation template across many accounts and Regions for consistent DR infrastructure?
options: AWS Service Catalog portfolios only
AWS Config aggregators
AWS Trusted Advisor
AWS CloudFormation StackSets
questions.explanation: StackSets deploy and manage stacks across accounts and Regions from one operation, integrated with Organizations. Service Catalog governs self-service products. Config aggregators collect compliance data. Trusted Advisor gives recommendations.

questions.question: A company runs its primary workload in a Region and needs its DNS to keep resolving and failing over even if Route 53 control plane in us-east-1 is impaired. Which statement is correct?
options: DNS resolution stops if the Route 53 control plane in us-east-1 is impaired, so failover must be avoided.
Health checks can only be created or modified during an event via the console in us-east-1.
Route 53 must be replaced by a third-party DNS for multi-Region DR.

Route 53 health checks and DNS query answering are data-plane functions that continue to operate; design failover using pre-created records with health checks rather than API changes during the event.
questions.explanation: Route 53 data plane (queries and health checks) is globally distributed and designed for 100% availability SLA; the control plane (record changes) is in us-east-1. Pre-configuring failover records avoids control-plane dependency. DNS resolution does not stop, and third-party DNS is unnecessary.

questions.question: A company uses Amazon FSx for Windows File Server for a critical file share. The share must remain available if an AZ fails. Which deployment type should be chosen?
options: Single-AZ 1 deployment
Multi-AZ deployment
Scratch deployment
Single-AZ 2 deployment with daily backups
questions.explanation: FSx for Windows Multi-AZ provisions an active and standby file server in separate AZs with automatic failover. Single-AZ options (including with backups) do not survive AZ loss. Scratch is a Lustre concept for temporary storage.

questions.question: A developer wants API Gateway to protect the backend from sudden traffic bursts from a single client. What should be configured?
options: A CloudFront distribution in front of the API with a longer TTL so repeated requests are served from cache.
A larger Lambda memory size so the backend can handle bursts from a single client faster.
Usage plans with API keys and per-client throttling (rate and burst limits).
A private API endpoint so that only clients inside the VPC can reach the backend.
questions.explanation: Usage plans apply throttling and quotas per API key, protecting the backend from noisy clients. Caching helps only cacheable GETs. Lambda memory is unrelated. Private endpoints restrict network access, not rate.

questions.question: A company needs to fail over a multi-tier application to another Region and wants a managed service that continuously checks readiness (quotas, capacity, configuration) of the recovery environment. Which feature should they use?
options: AWS Trusted Advisor service limits check only, reviewed weekly for each Region used for recovery.
Amazon Inspector continuous scanning of the recovery environment resources.
Amazon Application Recovery Controller readiness checks (together with routing controls).
AWS X-Ray service map of the recovery environment to verify dependencies.
questions.explanation: ARC readiness checks continuously audit that replica resources match production in capacity, quotas, and configuration; routing controls then shift traffic. Trusted Advisor checks quotas but not cross-Region replica readiness. Inspector scans vulnerabilities. X-Ray traces requests.

questions.question: A company wants to host a WordPress site with minimal effort and occasional traffic spikes. It must survive AZ failure. Which is MOST appropriate?
options: A single Lightsail instance with a static IP and automatic daily snapshots enabled for recovery.
A single large EC2 instance with MySQL installed locally, EBS snapshots taken every hour, and an Elastic IP for the site.
EC2 Auto Scaling across multiple AZs behind an ALB, with Amazon RDS Multi-AZ (or Aurora) and Amazon EFS for shared wp-content.
An S3 static website hosting the WordPress files behind a CloudFront distribution.
questions.explanation: Multi-AZ web tier, managed Multi-AZ database, and shared EFS storage remove single points of failure. A single Lightsail or EC2 instance is not resilient to AZ failure. WordPress is dynamic and cannot be hosted purely on S3 static hosting.

questions.question: A read-heavy application on Amazon RDS for MySQL shows high CPU from repeated identical product-catalog queries. The data changes a few times per day. What is the MOST effective way to reduce database load?
options: Enable Multi-AZ on the RDS instance so the standby can absorb read traffic during peaks.
Add an Amazon ElastiCache (Valkey/Redis OSS) cache using the cache-aside pattern with a TTL.
Switch the database storage from gp3 to io2 Block Express to raise provisioned IOPS for the catalog queries.
Increase the backup retention period.
questions.explanation: Caching repeated reads in ElastiCache offloads the database and gives sub-millisecond reads; TTL handles infrequent changes. Multi-AZ standby does not serve reads for a DB instance deployment. Storage IOPS is not the bottleneck (CPU from repeated queries is). Backup retention is unrelated.

questions.question: A DynamoDB table serves a product catalog with millions of reads per second on a small set of hot items, and needs microsecond read latency. What should be added?
options: A global secondary index on the partition key.
DynamoDB Streams.
Switching to provisioned capacity with auto scaling.
DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX).
questions.explanation: DAX is an in-memory, write-through cache for DynamoDB delivering microsecond reads with API compatibility. A GSI on the same key does not add caching. Streams capture changes. Capacity mode changes throughput billing but not microsecond latency.

questions.question: Users worldwide upload large video files (5–20 GB) to a single S3 bucket in us-east-1 and experience slow uploads. What should be used to improve upload speed?
options: S3 Transfer Acceleration combined with multipart upload.
S3 Cross-Region Replication to a bucket on each user continent.
Amazon CloudFront with a longer TTL on the upload path.
S3 Intelligent-Tiering.
questions.explanation: Transfer Acceleration routes uploads over the AWS edge network, and multipart uploads parallelize parts (required above 5 GB). CRR copies after upload. CloudFront TTL affects caching downloads. Intelligent-Tiering affects storage cost.

questions.question: An application reads S3 objects at 20,000 GET requests per second, all under a single prefix, and sees 503 Slow Down errors. What change helps MOST?
options: Enable S3 Versioning.
Move the objects to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, which is designed for millisecond reads of large volumes of data.
Spread objects across multiple prefixes; S3 scales to at least 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per prefix.
Enable default encryption with SSE-KMS so each GET uses a cached data key and is served faster.
questions.explanation: S3 scales per prefix (3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE and 5,500 GET/HEAD per second per prefix); spreading keys lets S3 partition. Versioning and storage class do not raise request rates. SSE-KMS adds KMS request quotas and can worsen throttling.

questions.question: A machine learning team needs a POSIX file system that delivers hundreds of GB/s throughput to thousands of GPU instances, linked to training data in S3. Which storage fits BEST?
options: Amazon FSx for Lustre with an S3 data repository association.
Amazon EFS with Elastic throughput mode and Max I/O performance.
Amazon EBS io2 Block Express volumes with Multi-Attach.
S3 Standard accessed directly via GetObject.
questions.explanation: FSx for Lustre is a parallel file system scaling to hundreds of GB/s and millions of IOPS with lazy loading from and export to S3. EFS scales but not to Lustre-level HPC throughput. EBS Multi-Attach is limited to 16 instances in one AZ. Direct S3 access is not POSIX.

questions.question: A database on EC2 needs 60,000 IOPS and 1,500 MiB/s throughput on a single volume at the lowest cost. Which EBS volume type is MOST cost-effective today?
options: io2 Block Express provisioned at 60,000 IOPS, because only io2 volumes can exceed 16,000 IOPS on a single volume.
st1 Throughput Optimized HDD.
gp2 sized large enough to reach 60,000 IOPS.
gp3, which now supports up to 80,000 IOPS and 2,000 MiB/s per volume, provisioned independently of size.
questions.explanation: Since September 2025 gp3 volumes support up to 64 TiB, 80,000 IOPS, and 2,000 MiB/s, making gp3 cheaper than io2 for this profile when sub-millisecond io2 durability/latency guarantees are not required. st1 is HDD and cannot deliver this IOPS. gp2 maxes at 16,000 IOPS.

questions.question: A global mobile game needs to route UDP traffic to the nearest healthy Regional endpoint with static anycast IP addresses and fast failover. What should be used?
options: Amazon CloudFront.
AWS Global Accelerator.
Route 53 latency-based routing only.
An Application Load Balancer with cross-zone load balancing.
questions.explanation: Global Accelerator provides two static anycast IPs, supports TCP and UDP, routes over the AWS backbone, and fails over in seconds without DNS caching issues. CloudFront is HTTP(S)-focused caching. Route 53 relies on DNS TTLs. ALB is Regional and HTTP only.

questions.question: An analytics team runs ad hoc SQL over 200 TB of CSV logs in S3 with Athena and complains about cost and slowness. What will MOST improve performance and cost?
options: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration.
Move the data to S3 Standard-IA, which lowers the storage cost and lets Athena scan it at a reduced per-TB query price.
Increase the Athena query timeout and use a larger workgroup so queries over the CSV data finish reliably.
Convert the data to compressed columnar Parquet/ORC and partition it (or use Apache Iceberg tables such as S3 Tables).
questions.explanation: Athena charges by data scanned; columnar compressed and partitioned data reduces bytes scanned dramatically. Iceberg/S3 Tables adds compaction and table maintenance. Transfer Acceleration is for uploads. Standard-IA adds retrieval fees. Timeouts do not improve speed.

questions.question: A web application has high latency for users in Asia; the origin is in us-east-1 and responses are mostly dynamic API calls. Which solution improves performance with LEAST changes?
options: Increase the instance size in us-east-1 and enable enhanced networking so each API response is generated faster.
Use S3 Transfer Acceleration.
Put CloudFront in front of the API (caching disabled for dynamic paths) to terminate TLS at the edge and use the AWS backbone.
Add Aurora read replicas in us-east-1 and point the read-heavy API paths at the reader endpoint to cut response times for Asian users.
questions.explanation: CloudFront improves dynamic content performance through edge TLS termination, persistent connections, and backbone routing even when not caching. Bigger instances do not reduce network latency. Transfer Acceleration is for S3. Same-Region replicas do not help geographic latency.

questions.question: An application requires the lowest possible network latency between tightly coupled HPC nodes. Which EC2 feature should be used?
options: A spread placement group.
A partition placement group across AZs so each node gets its own rack and network path.
A cluster placement group with instances that support Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA).
Instances in different AZs for resilience, connected through the AWS backbone.
questions.explanation: Cluster placement groups pack instances in a single AZ on low-latency, high-bandwidth networking; EFA adds OS-bypass for MPI. Spread and partition groups optimize for failure isolation, not latency. Multi-AZ increases latency.

questions.question: A SaaS company serves read-heavy traffic from Aurora MySQL. Read traffic grows unpredictably 20x during events. Which solution scales reads automatically with minimal management?
options: Create RDS for MySQL cross-Region read replicas and distribute reads with Route 53 weighted records.
Scale the writer to the largest instance class and enable Aurora Parallel Query for the read traffic.
Add Aurora Replicas with Aurora Auto Scaling (or Serverless v2 readers) behind the reader endpoint.
Enable Aurora Backtrack.
questions.explanation: Aurora supports up to 15 replicas on shared storage, and Auto Scaling or Serverless v2 readers adjust capacity; the reader endpoint load-balances. Cross-Region replicas add lag and are not for local scaling. A bigger writer does not scale reads horizontally. Backtrack rewinds data.

questions.question: A company processes streaming clickstream data and needs results in near real time, with multiple consumers reading the same stream at 2 MB/s each without contention. Which feature should be used?
options: Standard shared-throughput GetRecords polling for all consumers.
SQS standard queue.
Data Firehose buffering to S3.
Kinesis Data Streams enhanced fan-out consumers.
questions.explanation: Enhanced fan-out gives each registered consumer a dedicated 2 MB/s per shard via push (SubscribeToShard). Shared polling splits 2 MB/s per shard across all consumers. SQS delivers each message to one consumer. Firehose buffers for delivery and is not low-latency multi-consumer.

questions.question: A team needs to load streaming data into S3, Redshift, and OpenSearch with no code and automatic scaling, and can tolerate delays of about a minute. Which service is BEST?
options: Kinesis Data Streams with custom consumers.
Amazon Data Firehose.
Amazon SQS.
AWS Glue crawlers.
questions.explanation: Firehose is fully managed delivery to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch, Iceberg tables, and more with buffering and transformation. KDS requires writing consumers. SQS is not a delivery stream. Glue crawlers catalog data, they do not ingest streams.

questions.question: A retailer needs a data warehouse that runs complex joins over 50 TB with unpredictable, spiky query demand and no capacity management. Which option fits BEST?
options: A provisioned Redshift cluster sized for peak.
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with read replicas.
Amazon DynamoDB with PartiQL.
Amazon Redshift Serverless.
questions.explanation: Redshift Serverless automatically provisions and scales compute (RPUs) and charges for usage, ideal for spiky warehouse workloads. Provisioned-for-peak wastes cost. RDS is OLTP, not MPP analytics. DynamoDB is not designed for complex analytic joins.

questions.question: A serverless API built on Lambda has cold-start latency spikes that violate a p99 SLA for a Java function. Which option reduces cold starts MOST directly?
options: Increase the function timeout.
Enable Lambda SnapStart (or configure provisioned concurrency) for the function.
Move the function into a VPC.
Use an SQS trigger instead of API Gateway so requests are buffered while functions warm up.
questions.explanation: SnapStart restores from a cached snapshot of the initialized execution environment, and provisioned concurrency keeps environments pre-initialized. Timeout does not affect init. VPC placement does not reduce cold starts. Changing the trigger changes the API semantics.

questions.question: An application needs full-text search with relevance ranking and faceting over product descriptions stored in DynamoDB. What should be added?
options: Amazon OpenSearch Service (or OpenSearch Serverless) fed via the DynamoDB zero-ETL integration.
A DynamoDB global secondary index on the description attribute with a begins_with key condition.
Amazon Athena queries on DynamoDB exports.
ElastiCache for Memcached.
questions.explanation: OpenSearch provides full-text search, relevance, and aggregations; the zero-ETL integration keeps it in sync with DynamoDB. GSIs support key-based lookup, not full-text. Athena on exports is batch. Memcached is a key-value cache.

questions.question: A company needs single-digit millisecond key-value reads at 1M requests per second and wants each request to automatically route to the nearest Region for global users. Which architecture fits?
options: A single-Region Aurora cluster with 15 replicas.
An S3 bucket with Multi-Region Access Points serving a JSON object per key from the nearest bucket replica.
DynamoDB global tables in the user Regions, with Route 53 latency-based routing to Regional API endpoints.
RDS Proxy in each Region pointing at a single RDS instance, pooling connections to keep reads fast.
questions.explanation: Global tables provide local reads/writes in each Region at scale; latency routing sends users to the closest Region. A single-Region Aurora cannot provide local latency globally. S3 is not designed for millisecond key-value OLTP. RDS Proxy pools connections but data is still in one Region.

questions.question: A Lambda function connects to RDS and exhausts database connections during traffic spikes. What is the BEST fix?
options: Increase the RDS max_connections parameter to 100,000.
Increase Lambda reserved concurrency to 1,000.
Move the function outside the VPC.
Use Amazon RDS Proxy between Lambda and the database.
questions.explanation: RDS Proxy pools and shares connections, protecting the database from connection storms and supporting IAM auth. Raising max_connections is bounded by memory. More concurrency makes it worse. Network placement does not fix connection counts.

questions.question: An EC2-hosted application writes logs locally and needs 1 million small random IOPS on temporary scratch data that can be lost. Which storage is BEST?
options: EBS sc1 volumes.
Amazon EFS.
Amazon S3 Standard.
EC2 instance store NVMe volumes on a storage-optimized instance (for example i4i/i8g).
questions.explanation: Instance store NVMe provides extremely high random IOPS at no extra cost, suitable for ephemeral scratch data. sc1 is cold HDD. EFS and S3 are network storage with higher latency.

questions.question: A company runs a GraphQL API for a mobile app with real-time updates to connected clients and multiple data sources (DynamoDB, Lambda, HTTP). Which service reduces custom code MOST?
options: API Gateway REST API with Lambda proxy integration and a WebSocket API for pushing updates.
An ALB in front of EC2 Auto Scaling running Apollo Server with a Redis pub/sub layer for subscriptions.
Amazon SNS mobile push only.
AWS AppSync with resolvers for each data source and GraphQL subscriptions (or AppSync Events).
questions.explanation: AppSync is managed GraphQL with built-in real-time subscriptions over WebSockets and direct resolvers to DynamoDB, Lambda, HTTP, and more. REST with Lambda requires building GraphQL and real-time yourself. Self-hosted Apollo adds ops. SNS push is notifications, not a data API.

questions.question: A company wants to right-size EC2 instances and EBS volumes based on actual utilization metrics. Which service provides ML-based recommendations?
options: AWS Compute Optimizer.
AWS Budgets.
AWS CloudTrail.
Amazon Inspector.
questions.explanation: Compute Optimizer analyzes CloudWatch metrics to recommend optimal EC2, ASG, EBS, Lambda, ECS on Fargate, and RDS configurations. Budgets tracks spend. CloudTrail logs API calls. Inspector finds vulnerabilities.

questions.question: Which EC2 instance family should be chosen for a memory-bound in-memory database needing high memory per vCPU?
options: Compute optimized (C family).
Memory optimized (R or X families).
Burstable (T family).
Accelerated computing (P family).
questions.explanation: R and X families provide high memory-to-vCPU ratios for in-memory databases and caches (X8aedz offers up to 3 TiB). C is for compute-bound work. T instances are burstable for low average CPU. P instances are GPUs.

questions.question: A company wants the best price performance for a general-purpose Linux fleet running Java microservices and is willing to rebuild images for ARM. What should they choose?
options: x86 instances with hyperthreading disabled.
Mac instances.
GPU instances for all services.
AWS Graviton-based instances (for example the latest Graviton4/Graviton5 generation).
questions.explanation: Graviton instances offer the best price performance in EC2 for most general-purpose workloads, and Java runs well on ARM64; Graviton5 was announced at re:Invent 2025. Disabling hyperthreading reduces capacity. Mac and GPU instances are specialized and costly.

questions.question: An application running on EC2 frequently reads the same configuration values from Systems Manager Parameter Store and is being throttled. What should be done?
options: Cache parameter values in the application (for example with the Parameters and Secrets extension) and enable higher throughput.
Move the parameters into a JSON object in S3 and read it on every request, since S3 supports thousands of GET requests per second per prefix.
Store the parameters in instance user data and re-read them from the metadata service on every request.
Create a new parameter for every request.
questions.explanation: Caching avoids repeated API calls; Parameter Store also offers a higher-throughput setting. Reading S3 per request adds latency. User data is not for runtime config and is not secure. Creating parameters per request is nonsensical.

questions.question: A workload performs large sequential reads for big data processing on EC2 and needs low cost per GB with high throughput. Which EBS type fits?
options: st1 (Throughput Optimized HDD).
io2 Block Express.
gp3 at maximum IOPS.
sc1 (Cold HDD).
questions.explanation: st1 is optimized for frequently accessed, throughput-intensive sequential workloads at low cost. io2 is for IOPS-intensive latency-sensitive databases. gp3 max performance costs more for this pattern. sc1 is for infrequently accessed data with lower throughput.

questions.question: An online retailer requires sub-10 ms responses for personalized product recommendations using vector similarity across 50 million embeddings with frequent updates and high QPS. Which option fits BEST?
options: Amazon S3 Vectors, querying the vector index directly from the recommendation service on every page view.
Amazon OpenSearch Service vector engine (optionally GPU-accelerated) or Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector.
Amazon Athena with a UDF computing cosine similarity over embeddings stored as Parquet in S3.
Amazon Redshift with a full table scan.
questions.explanation: OpenSearch (and pgvector) provide in-memory ANN indexes for low-latency, high-QPS vector search. S3 Vectors optimizes cost with ~100 ms-class latencies and is best for less frequent queries or large, cold vector sets. Athena and Redshift scans are far too slow.

questions.question: A company wants its API Gateway REST API to respond faster for repeated GET requests with identical parameters. What should be enabled?
options: API Gateway stage caching with an appropriate TTL.
Usage plans.
Request validation.
Mutual TLS.
questions.explanation: Stage-level caching returns cached responses for identical requests up to the TTL (default 300 s, max 3600 s). Usage plans throttle. Validation checks requests. mTLS secures clients.

questions.question: An application must decouple a producer that sends 50,000 messages per second from consumers, with at-least-once delivery and no ordering requirement. Which queue type is appropriate?
options: SQS FIFO queue without high throughput mode.
Amazon MQ single-instance broker.
SNS FIFO topic.
SQS standard queue.
questions.explanation: Standard queues support nearly unlimited throughput with at-least-once delivery. FIFO without high throughput mode is limited (300 API calls/s, 3,000 with batching). A single MQ broker has limited scale and is not HA. SNS FIFO is for ordered fan-out.

questions.question: A company runs Spark ETL jobs nightly on a persistent EMR cluster that sits idle 18 hours a day. They want to keep Spark but remove cluster management and idle cost. What should they use?
options: A larger persistent EMR cluster with instance fleets.
Amazon Redshift provisioned.
Amazon EMR Serverless (or AWS Glue for Spark jobs).
Amazon Athena for all transformation logic.
questions.explanation: EMR Serverless runs Spark/Hive jobs with automatic scaling and no idle cluster; Glue is also serverless Spark. A bigger cluster increases idle cost. Redshift is a warehouse, not a Spark runtime. Athena SQL may not cover existing Spark logic.

questions.question: A static single-page application is hosted on S3. Users report slow loads globally. What is the MOST effective improvement?
options: Serve the site through CloudFront with Origin Access Control to the S3 bucket.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration for downloads.
Move the bucket to a Region closer to the developers and enable S3 Transfer Acceleration.
Use S3 One Zone-IA.
questions.explanation: CloudFront caches the assets at 750+ points of presence and OAC keeps the bucket private. Transfer Acceleration is for uploads/transfers, not a CDN. Moving Regions helps only one geography. One Zone-IA reduces cost, not latency.

questions.question: A Lambda function performs CPU-intensive image processing and takes 40 seconds at 1,024 MB memory. What is the simplest way to reduce duration?
options: Increase the timeout to 15 minutes.
Increase the memory setting, since Lambda allocates CPU in proportion to memory (up to 6 vCPUs).
Enable provisioned concurrency so each invocation starts on a pre-warmed, faster execution environment.
Add an SQS dead-letter queue.
questions.explanation: More memory gives more CPU, often reducing duration enough to lower total cost. Timeout does not speed execution. Provisioned concurrency only removes cold starts. DLQs are for failure handling.

questions.question: An enterprise has a 20 TB MySQL database with write-heavy workloads that has hit vertical scaling limits. They need horizontal write scaling while remaining on a managed relational service with minimal application changes. Which option is BEST?
options: Add Aurora Replicas and enable write forwarding so the replicas share the write load with the writer instance across all AZs.
Enable Multi-AZ with two readable standbys so writes are distributed across three AZs.
Aurora PostgreSQL Limitless Database if moving to PostgreSQL is acceptable; otherwise shard across multiple Aurora MySQL clusters.
Move the database to Amazon Redshift, whose massively parallel architecture distributes inserts and updates across many compute nodes.
questions.explanation: Aurora Limitless Database provides managed horizontal write scaling via sharded tables for PostgreSQL; for MySQL, sharding across clusters is the typical approach. Replicas scale reads, not writes (write forwarding still sends every write to the single writer). Multi-AZ is for HA. Redshift is analytic, not OLTP.

questions.question: A time-series IoT application needs to store trillions of data points with automatic tiering between a memory store and a magnetic store, and built-in time-series functions. Which database fits?
options: Amazon Timestream.
Amazon Neptune.
Amazon DocumentDB.
Amazon QLDB.
questions.explanation: Timestream (LiveAnalytics, or Timestream for InfluxDB) is purpose-built for time-series with tiered storage and time functions. Neptune is graph. DocumentDB is JSON documents. QLDB is a ledger (and has been discontinued).

questions.question: A social network needs to query friend-of-friend relationships many hops deep with low latency. Which database is purpose-built for this?
options: Amazon DynamoDB.
Amazon Redshift.
Amazon Neptune.
Amazon Keyspaces.
questions.explanation: Neptune is a managed graph database supporting Gremlin, openCypher, and SPARQL for traversals. DynamoDB, Redshift, and Keyspaces require expensive joins or multiple lookups for deep relationship traversal.

questions.question: A container platform on ECS needs to scale out within seconds when request rates spike, but CloudWatch standard-resolution metrics introduce lag. What recent capability helps?
options: Switch the cluster capacity providers to EC2 Spot only, because Spot capacity launches faster than On-Demand during request spikes.
Disabling deployment circuit breaker.
ECS service auto scaling with high-resolution (20-second) metrics, which AWS reports improves scale-out time significantly.
Use ECS Exec to add tasks manually whenever the CloudWatch request-count dashboard shows a spike.
questions.explanation: AWS announced (Summit New York 2026) ECS auto scaling using 20-second high-resolution metrics, reported to improve scale-out time by 76%. Spot changes cost not reactivity. Circuit breaker is for deployments. Manual intervention defeats auto scaling.

questions.question: A company needs a managed Cassandra-compatible database without managing clusters. Which service fits?
options: Amazon DocumentDB.
Amazon Keyspaces (for Apache Cassandra).
Amazon ElastiCache.
Amazon Neptune.
questions.explanation: Keyspaces is serverless, CQL-compatible Cassandra. DocumentDB is MongoDB-compatible. ElastiCache is caching. Neptune is graph.

questions.question: Which S3 feature lets an application retrieve only a subset of data from a CSV object using SQL, reducing data transfer?
options: S3 Object Lambda with a function that parses the CSV and returns only the matching rows for all queries.
S3 Inventory.
S3 Batch Operations running a job that filters the CSV objects before each read.
Use Athena (or byte-range fetches of columnar files); S3 Select is closed to new customers.
questions.explanation: AWS closed S3 Select to new customers in 2024; the recommended path is Athena or reading columnar formats with range requests. Object Lambda transforms whole responses via code. Inventory lists objects. Batch Operations acts on many objects at once.
