questions.question: A company runs a latency-sensitive trading application that must reach users in a metro area with single-digit millisecond latency, where no AWS Region exists nearby. What should be used?
options: A CloudFront distribution with caching disabled.
Deploy in the nearest Region with larger instances.
AWS Local Zones in that metro area (or Outposts on-premises if data residency requires).
AWS Wavelength Zones for fixed-line users.
questions.explanation: Local Zones place compute, storage, and select services close to large metros for single-digit ms latency. CloudFront does not run the application compute. A distant Region still adds latency. Wavelength is for 5G mobile carrier networks.

questions.question: A mobile game needs ultra-low latency for users on 5G networks by placing compute at the telecom carrier edge. Which service applies?
options: AWS Local Zones.
AWS Outposts.
AWS Global Accelerator.
AWS Wavelength.
questions.explanation: Wavelength Zones embed AWS compute in carrier 5G networks, avoiding internet hops. Local Zones are metro extensions not inside carrier networks. Outposts are on-premises racks. Global Accelerator optimizes routing to Regions.

questions.question: A developer notices a DynamoDB table throttling writes because one partition key value receives most traffic. What should be done?
options: Enable DynamoDB Streams so that writes are processed asynchronously and throttling is avoided.
Add a local secondary index on the hot attribute so that the table writes are distributed across additional storage partitions.
Redesign the partition key for higher cardinality (e.g., add a random or calculated suffix) so writes spread out.
Enable PITR.
questions.explanation: Hot partitions are fixed by distributing writes across many key values. Streams, LSIs, and PITR do not change partition distribution.

questions.question: A company wants a relational analytics copy of operational Aurora MySQL data in Redshift within seconds, without building ETL pipelines. What should they use?
options: AWS DMS full load nightly.
Aurora zero-ETL integration with Amazon Redshift.
AWS Glue crawlers every hour.
Export snapshots to S3 and COPY into Redshift.
questions.explanation: Zero-ETL integrations replicate transactional data into Redshift in near real time with no pipeline to manage. DMS and snapshot exports add latency and operations. Glue crawlers only update metadata.

questions.question: An ALB distributes traffic to EC2 targets. Some requests take 30 seconds and the team wants new instances to receive traffic gradually after launch. What should be enabled?
options: Cross-zone load balancing disabled.
Slow start mode on the target group (or the automatic target weights algorithm).
Connection draining set to 0.
Sticky sessions with a 1-day duration so existing users stay on warmed-up instances.
questions.explanation: Slow start ramps up the share of requests to newly registered targets. Disabling cross-zone, removing draining, or long stickiness do not provide gradual warm-up and can harm availability.

questions.question: A company needs to run a containerized web app with automatic HTTPS URL, load balancing, and auto scaling from just a container image, with the least configuration. Which option fits BEST?
options: Amazon EKS with self-managed node groups.
EC2 instances with Docker installed.
Amazon ECS Express Mode.
AWS Batch.
questions.explanation: ECS Express Mode (launched November 2025) creates a Fargate service, ALB with TLS, an AWS-provided URL, and auto scaling from just an image at no additional charge. AWS App Runner stopped accepting new customers on April 30, 2026 and AWS recommends ECS Express Mode instead. EKS and raw EC2 require far more setup. Batch is for jobs, not web services.

questions.question: A genomics pipeline needs to run 10,000 containerized jobs with dependencies, using Spot capacity, retries, and job queues with priorities. Which service is MOST suitable?
options: AWS Lambda with 15-minute functions.
AWS Batch with managed compute environments using Spot and On-Demand.
Amazon ECS services with desired count 10,000.
Amazon EMR on EC2.
questions.explanation: AWS Batch manages job queues, dependencies, retries, and compute environments (EC2/Spot/Fargate/EKS). Lambda has 15-minute limits and resource caps. ECS services are for long-running services. EMR targets big data frameworks.

questions.question: A reporting dashboard queries Amazon Redshift and repeatedly runs the same aggregate queries every few seconds, while underlying tables change hourly. What improves response time with the LEAST effort?
options: Rely on Redshift result caching and materialized views with auto refresh for the aggregates.
Add more nodes to the cluster so the repeated aggregate queries scale linearly with cluster size.
Export the data to S3 nightly and query it with Athena from the dashboard instead of Redshift.
Enable concurrency scaling so repeated dashboard queries run on additional transient clusters.
questions.explanation: Result caching returns repeated identical queries instantly and materialized views precompute aggregates that refresh as data changes. Adding nodes costs more for the same repeated work. Moving to Athena adds data movement and scan cost. Concurrency scaling helps bursts of concurrent queries but does not avoid recomputing identical aggregates.

questions.question: An application on EC2 needs to read objects from an S3 bucket. The developers currently store an IAM user access key in a config file. What is the MOST secure approach?
options: Keep the access key in the config file but encrypt it with a KMS customer managed key and decrypt it at startup.
Store the access key in instance user data.
Attach an IAM role to the instance through an instance profile with least-privilege S3 permissions.
Make the bucket public and restrict by IP address.
questions.explanation: Instance roles deliver temporary, automatically rotated credentials via the instance metadata service, eliminating long-term keys. Encrypting keys still leaves long-term credentials to manage. User data is readable from the instance and not secret. Public buckets violate least privilege.

questions.question: A company must ensure that all objects uploaded to an S3 bucket are encrypted with a customer managed KMS key and that nobody can upload unencrypted objects. What should be configured?
options: Set default bucket encryption to SSE-KMS with the customer managed key and add a bucket policy that denies PutObject requests not using that key.
Enable S3 Versioning.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration.
Rely on the default SSE-S3 encryption that S3 applies to every new object, and enable S3 Versioning to keep an audit trail of uploads.
questions.explanation: Default SSE-KMS encryption with a bucket policy condition on s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id enforces the specific key. Versioning and Transfer Acceleration are unrelated. SSE-S3 is default for all new objects but uses S3-managed keys, not the customer managed key.

questions.question: An RDS database password is hard-coded in application code. The company wants automatic rotation every 30 days with no application downtime. Which service should be used?
options: Systems Manager Parameter Store SecureString standard parameters.
An environment variable in the Lambda function.
AWS Secrets Manager with managed rotation for the RDS secret.
AWS KMS key rotation.
questions.explanation: Secrets Manager stores and natively rotates RDS credentials on a schedule (RDS can also manage the master password in Secrets Manager). Parameter Store standard parameters have no built-in rotation. Environment variables are static. KMS rotation rotates key material, not database passwords.

questions.question: A company wants to prevent member accounts in AWS Organizations from disabling CloudTrail or leaving the organization. What should be used?
options: Attach an IAM permissions boundary to every IAM user and role in member accounts that omits CloudTrail and Organizations permissions.
Service control policies (SCPs) attached to the OUs that deny cloudtrail:StopLogging, cloudtrail:DeleteTrail, and organizations:LeaveOrganization.
AWS Config rules with auto-remediation only.
Tag policies.
questions.explanation: SCPs set maximum available permissions for all principals in member accounts, including root, and are the preventive guardrail. Permission boundaries apply per principal and can be forgotten. Config detects after the fact. Tag policies standardize tags.

questions.question: A web application behind an ALB is receiving SQL injection and cross-site scripting attempts. Which service mitigates these at the edge of the application?
options: AWS Shield Standard.
Security groups on the ALB that allow only ports 80 and 443 from the internet and block all other inbound ports.
AWS WAF with AWS Managed Rules (core rule set and SQL database rule group) attached to the ALB.
Amazon GuardDuty.
questions.explanation: WAF inspects HTTP requests and blocks common exploits like SQLi and XSS. Shield Standard protects against network/transport DDoS. Security groups work on ports and IPs, not payloads. GuardDuty detects threats but does not block requests.

questions.question: A company wants to detect compromised EC2 instances communicating with known command-and-control servers and unusual API calls. Which service provides this with minimal setup?
options: Amazon Inspector.
AWS Config.
Amazon Macie.
Amazon GuardDuty.
questions.explanation: GuardDuty analyzes CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs, and more for threats such as C2 traffic and credential misuse. Inspector scans for vulnerabilities. Config tracks configuration. Macie discovers sensitive data in S3.

questions.question: Which service automatically discovers and classifies sensitive data such as PII in Amazon S3?
options: Amazon Macie.
Amazon Detective.
AWS Security Hub.
Amazon Inspector.
questions.explanation: Macie uses ML and pattern matching to find sensitive data in S3. Detective investigates findings. Security Hub aggregates findings. Inspector scans workloads for vulnerabilities.

questions.question: A company needs to continuously scan EC2 instances, ECR container images, and Lambda functions for software vulnerabilities. Which service should be used?
options: Amazon Inspector.
Amazon GuardDuty.
AWS Trusted Advisor.
AWS Shield Advanced.
questions.explanation: Inspector automatically discovers and scans EC2, ECR images, and Lambda functions (including code) for CVEs and network exposure. GuardDuty detects threats. Trusted Advisor gives best-practice checks. Shield Advanced is DDoS protection.

questions.question: A company with 300 accounts wants a single place to view prioritized security risks, correlating findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, and CSPM checks, with exposure analysis. What should they use?
options: Build Amazon CloudWatch dashboards in every account that chart GuardDuty, Inspector, and Macie finding counts, and have the security team review them weekly.
AWS Security Hub (the re:Invent 2025 GA version with near real-time risk analytics) with a delegated administrator account across the organization.
AWS CloudTrail Lake only.
Amazon Detective in each account without aggregation.
questions.explanation: Security Hub centralizes and correlates findings across accounts and services, and the new version prioritizes exposures and risks; a delegated admin aggregates org-wide. Per-account dashboards do not correlate. CloudTrail Lake queries API events. Detective investigates rather than centrally prioritizes posture.

questions.question: A company wants to provide workforce users single sign-on to multiple AWS accounts using their existing Microsoft Entra ID identities. Which service should they use?
options: IAM users in every account.
AWS IAM Identity Center with Entra ID as an external identity provider (SAML + SCIM provisioning).
Amazon Cognito user pools federated with Entra ID through OIDC, with employees signing in to the AWS console through the hosted UI.
AWS Directory Service Simple AD.
questions.explanation: IAM Identity Center provides workforce SSO across Organizations accounts and applications with permission sets, federated to Entra ID. IAM users are long-term credentials per account. Cognito is for customer (CIAM) identities. Simple AD is a basic directory not integrated with Entra ID.

questions.question: A mobile app needs user sign-up, sign-in, MFA, and social login (Google, Apple) for millions of customers. Which service is designed for this?
options: AWS IAM Identity Center.
IAM users with MFA.
Amazon Cognito user pools.
AWS Directory Service for Microsoft AD.
questions.explanation: Cognito user pools provide customer identity (CIAM) with hosted UI/managed login, MFA, and social/OIDC/SAML federation at scale. Identity Center is for workforce. IAM users are not for app customers. Managed AD is for Windows workloads.

questions.question: A company wants to let developers create IAM roles for their applications but must prevent them from ever granting permissions beyond a defined set, including privilege escalation by creating new roles. What should be used?
options: IAM permissions boundaries, with a policy requiring that any role developers create has the boundary attached (iam:PermissionsBoundary condition).
An SCP that denies iam:CreateRole and iam:AttachRolePolicy for developers, so that only the central platform team can create or modify any IAM role in the accounts.
AWS Config rule to detect admin policies.
Resource-based policies on every resource.
questions.explanation: Permissions boundaries cap the maximum permissions of roles/users, and requiring the boundary on created roles prevents escalation. Denying CreateRole blocks the legitimate need. Config only detects. Resource policies do not limit the identity side.

questions.question: An S3 bucket must be accessible only through CloudFront and never directly. What is the recommended configuration?
options: Use CloudFront Origin Access Control (OAC) and a bucket policy that allows only the CloudFront service principal with the distribution ARN condition, keeping Block Public Access on.
Make the bucket public and use signed URLs.
Use an Origin Access Identity with a public bucket ACL.
Restrict the bucket by CloudFront edge IP ranges in the bucket policy.
questions.explanation: OAC is the current recommended method (successor to OAI), supporting SSE-KMS and all Regions; the bucket stays private. A public bucket can be bypassed. ACL-based public access defeats the purpose. Edge IP lists change and are brittle.

questions.question: A company needs to encrypt data at rest in EBS volumes and ensure all new volumes in the Region are encrypted automatically. What should be done?
options: Use instance store volumes.
Enable EBS encryption by default for the account in each Region (optionally with a customer managed KMS key).
Enable full-disk encryption inside the operating system with LUKS or BitLocker on every instance through a user data script.
Enable S3 default encryption.
questions.explanation: EBS encryption by default ensures all new volumes and snapshot copies are encrypted with KMS. Instance store is ephemeral and not the target. OS-level encryption is manual and inconsistent. S3 settings do not affect EBS.

questions.question: A security team requires that KMS keys used to encrypt a sensitive data lake can only be used by principals in the organization, and only via the S3 service. Which KMS key policy conditions achieve this?
options: Use aws:PrincipalOrgID to restrict to the organization and kms:ViaService set to the S3 service endpoint for the Region.
Use an aws:SourceIp condition with the corporate CIDR ranges so that only requests originating from company networks can use the key.
Enable automatic key rotation every 90 days.
Use an AWS managed key for S3 (aws/s3).
questions.explanation: aws:PrincipalOrgID limits usage to org principals and kms:ViaService ensures the key is only used through S3. SourceIp does not apply to service-originated calls. Rotation changes key material, not access. AWS managed keys have fixed key policies you cannot customize.

questions.question: A company wants all API calls across all accounts in its organization recorded to a central, tamper-resistant location. What should be configured?
options: A separate CloudTrail trail in each account writing to a local S3 bucket owned by that account administrators, with versioning so deleted logs can be recovered.
VPC Flow Logs in every VPC.
CloudWatch Logs Insights queries.
An organization trail in CloudTrail delivering to a centralized S3 bucket in a log archive account, with log file validation and S3 Object Lock.
questions.explanation: An organization trail captures events from all accounts centrally; log file validation detects tampering and Object Lock prevents deletion. Per-account trails are harder to govern. Flow logs capture network traffic, not API calls. Logs Insights queries existing logs.

questions.question: An application in a private subnet must access S3 without traversing the internet or a NAT gateway. What should be used?
options: An S3 gateway VPC endpoint with a route table entry and an endpoint policy.
An internet gateway attached to the private subnet.
A VPN connection to S3.
An Elastic IP address on each instance and a route through the internet gateway restricted to the S3 IP prefixes.
questions.explanation: Gateway endpoints route S3 (and DynamoDB) traffic over the AWS network at no additional cost, and endpoint policies restrict access. An IGW makes subnets public. VPN is for on-premises connectivity. Elastic IPs require public connectivity.

questions.question: A company must ensure that its S3 buckets can only be accessed from its own VPC endpoints and from identities in its organization, forming a data perimeter. Which combination is MOST appropriate?
options: Security groups on the buckets.
Network ACLs on the S3 service.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration.

Bucket policies with aws:SourceVpce / aws:PrincipalOrgID conditions, VPC endpoint policies restricting to org resources (aws:ResourceOrgID), and SCPs or resource control policies (RCPs) to enforce at scale.
questions.explanation: Data perimeters combine identity, resource, and network controls: resource policies/RCPs for trusted identities and networks, endpoint policies for trusted resources, and SCPs for identity-side limits. S3 does not have security groups or NACLs. Transfer Acceleration is unrelated.

questions.question: An application must use TLS certificates for a public ALB that renew automatically. Which service provides this at no additional cost for public certificates?
options: AWS Secrets Manager.
AWS KMS.
AWS Certificate Manager (ACM).
IAM server certificates uploaded with the AWS CLI.
questions.explanation: ACM issues and auto-renews public TLS certificates for integrated services like ELB, CloudFront, and API Gateway at no extra cost. Secrets Manager stores secrets. KMS manages keys. IAM server certificates are legacy and do not auto-renew.

questions.question: A company is subject to a large DDoS attack on its CloudFront and Route 53 hosted application and wants 24/7 access to the Shield Response Team and cost protection for scaling charges. What should they subscribe to?
options: AWS Shield Standard.
AWS WAF only.
AWS Shield Advanced.
Amazon GuardDuty.
questions.explanation: Shield Advanced adds enhanced detection, SRT access, and DDoS cost protection. Shield Standard is automatic and free but lacks SRT and cost protection. WAF handles layer 7 rules but not the full service. GuardDuty is threat detection.

questions.question: A company must allow a third-party SaaS vendor to access an S3 bucket in its account. How should cross-account access be granted securely while preventing the confused deputy problem?
options: Create a dedicated IAM user for the vendor with an S3-only policy and share its long-term access keys with the vendor through an encrypted channel.
Make the bucket public with a random name.
Create an IAM role trusted by the vendor account with an sts:ExternalId condition, granting least-privilege S3 access.
Share the root account credentials with MFA.
questions.explanation: A role assumed with an external ID prevents another vendor customer from tricking the vendor into accessing your resources. Sharing long-term keys or root credentials is insecure. Public buckets expose data to everyone.

questions.question: Which statement about security groups is correct?
options: Security groups are stateless and require explicit outbound rules for return traffic.
Security groups support both allow and deny rules evaluated in order.
Security groups apply at the subnet level.
Security groups are stateful and support allow rules only; return traffic is automatically allowed.
questions.explanation: Security groups are stateful allow-only firewalls at the ENI level. Network ACLs are stateless, support allow and deny, evaluate rules in number order, and apply at the subnet level.

questions.question: A company wants to block a specific malicious IP range from reaching instances in a subnet. Which control is appropriate?
options: A security group rule on the instances that explicitly denies inbound traffic from the malicious CIDR range.
An IAM policy with aws:SourceIp.
A route table blackhole to the internet gateway.
A network ACL deny rule on the subnet (or an AWS WAF IP set for HTTP traffic at the ALB).
questions.explanation: Network ACLs support explicit deny rules at the subnet boundary; WAF IP sets block at layer 7. Security groups cannot deny. IAM policies govern API calls, not network traffic. Removing IGW routes would affect all traffic.

questions.question: A company wants to centrally inspect all east-west and egress traffic between VPCs with stateful rules and domain filtering. Which architecture fits BEST?
options: AWS Network Firewall in a centralized inspection VPC attached to Transit Gateway (with appliance mode enabled).
Security groups on every instance that reference each other across VPCs, with outbound rules restricted to approved destinations.
NACLs on every subnet.
AWS WAF on each NAT gateway.
questions.explanation: Network Firewall provides stateful inspection, Suricata rules, and domain filtering; a centralized inspection VPC with TGW routes all inter-VPC and egress traffic through it, and appliance mode keeps flows symmetric. Security groups/NACLs do not provide deep inspection or FQDN filtering. WAF cannot attach to NAT gateways.

questions.question: An organization wants to evaluate whether resources comply with rules such as "EBS volumes must be encrypted" and keep a configuration history. Which service should be used?
options: AWS CloudTrail with an organization trail and CloudTrail Lake queries.
Amazon Inspector.
AWS Budgets.
AWS Config with managed rules (and conformance packs).
questions.explanation: Config records resource configurations over time and evaluates compliance rules, with optional auto-remediation via SSM Automation. CloudTrail records API calls. Inspector scans vulnerabilities. Budgets tracks spend.

questions.question: A new multi-account landing zone is needed with preconfigured guardrails, centralized logging, account vending, and drift detection, using AWS best practices with minimal custom build. Which service should be used?
options: AWS Organizations alone with manual SCPs.
AWS Service Catalog alone.
AWS CloudFormation StackSets alone.
AWS Control Tower.
questions.explanation: Control Tower orchestrates Organizations, IAM Identity Center, CloudTrail, Config, and account factory to deliver a governed landing zone with preventive, detective, and proactive controls. The other services are building blocks requiring custom assembly.

questions.question: A company wants users in an Amazon Cognito user pool to access S3 directly from a mobile app with temporary, scoped AWS credentials. What should be used?
options: Embed IAM user access keys in the app.
Cognito identity pools that exchange user pool tokens for temporary IAM role credentials.
Make the S3 bucket public.
IAM Identity Center permission sets assigned to each app user, with the app calling the access portal to get credentials.
questions.explanation: Identity pools (federated identities) issue temporary credentials mapped to IAM roles, optionally with per-user prefixes. Embedded keys are extractable. Public buckets expose data. Identity Center is for workforce users.

questions.question: Which KMS feature lets a company control and hold the key material in its own on-premises HSMs while still integrating with AWS services?
options: AWS managed keys (aws/service keys).
AWS KMS External Key Store (XKS).
Automatic key rotation.
SSE-S3.
questions.explanation: XKS keeps key material in an external key manager outside AWS, used by KMS for cryptographic operations. AWS managed keys are fully controlled by AWS. Rotation is a lifecycle feature. SSE-S3 uses S3-managed keys.

questions.question: An auditor requires that security findings, CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and Route 53 resolver logs from all accounts be normalized into a common schema in a customer-owned data lake. Which service fits?
options: Amazon Macie.
AWS Audit Manager assessments that collect evidence from CloudTrail and Config into framework reports.
CloudWatch Logs in each account.
Amazon Security Lake, which normalizes data to OCSF in Apache Parquet stored in your S3 buckets.
questions.explanation: Security Lake centralizes security data from AWS and third-party sources into OCSF format in S3 across accounts and Regions. Macie classifies sensitive data. Audit Manager collects evidence for frameworks. Per-account CloudWatch Logs are not normalized or centralized.

questions.question: An application must give temporary download links for private S3 objects to authenticated users that expire in 15 minutes. What should be used?
options: S3 presigned URLs generated by the backend with a 15-minute expiry.
Public-read ACL on each object.
S3 Transfer Acceleration.
A bucket policy allowing all principals s3:GetObject on a random, unguessable prefix.
questions.explanation: Presigned URLs grant time-limited access using the signer permissions. Public ACLs and open bucket policies expose objects permanently. Transfer Acceleration affects speed only.

questions.question: A company wants to enforce MFA for sensitive API actions such as deleting S3 buckets. Which IAM condition key is used?
options: aws:SecureTransport.
aws:RequestedRegion.
aws:PrincipalTag.
aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent (or aws:MultiFactorAuthAge) in a policy condition.
questions.explanation: MFA condition keys ensure the request was made with MFA-authenticated credentials. SecureTransport requires TLS. RequestedRegion restricts Regions. PrincipalTag enables ABAC.

questions.question: A company wants to scale access control across hundreds of projects without writing a policy per project. Engineers and resources are tagged with project names. Which approach fits BEST?
options: Create one IAM group and customer managed policy per project, adding engineers to the right groups through the identity provider and updating them as projects change.
Attribute-based access control (ABAC) using aws:PrincipalTag and aws:ResourceTag conditions, with tags from IAM Identity Center/IdP session tags.
Use resource-based policies with explicit ARNs for every resource.
Use SCPs per project.
questions.explanation: ABAC matches principal tags to resource tags, so one policy scales across projects and new resources automatically. Per-project groups and ARN-specific policies grow linearly. SCPs are guardrails, not fine-grained grants.

questions.question: An API Gateway REST API must be accessible only from within a company VPC and never from the internet. What should be configured?
options: A private API endpoint accessed via an interface VPC endpoint (execute-api) with a resource policy restricting to that endpoint.
An edge-optimized endpoint with a WAF rule.
A Regional endpoint with an API key.
A public Regional endpoint with a Lambda authorizer that rejects any request whose source IP is outside the corporate VPC CIDR ranges and NAT gateway IPs.
questions.explanation: Private APIs are reachable only through interface VPC endpoints; resource policies restrict which VPCs/endpoints. Edge or Regional endpoints are internet-facing even with WAF, API keys, or authorizers.

questions.question: Which is the recommended way to protect the AWS account root user?
options: Use the root user daily for admin tasks with a strong password.
Create access keys for the root user for automation.

Enable MFA on the root user, remove root access keys, and use it only for tasks that require root; in Organizations, consider centralized root access management to remove member account root credentials.
Share root credentials with the operations team.
questions.explanation: Best practice is to lock down root with MFA, no access keys, and minimal use; Organizations now supports centrally managing (and removing) root credentials in member accounts. Daily use, root keys, and sharing are all anti-patterns.

questions.question: A company wants to verify that its IAM policies do not grant public or cross-account access to resources and wants to find unused permissions to tighten roles. Which service provides both?
options: AWS Trusted Advisor security checks (for example exposed access keys and S3 bucket permissions).
Amazon Detective.
IAM Access Analyzer (external access analysis and unused access analysis).
AWS Artifact.
questions.explanation: Access Analyzer uses automated reasoning to find resources shared externally and identifies unused roles, keys, and permissions; it can also generate policies from CloudTrail. Trusted Advisor has limited checks. Detective investigates incidents. Artifact provides compliance reports.

questions.question: An organization wants to provide zero-trust access to internal web applications for remote employees without a VPN, evaluating identity and device posture per request. Which service fits?
options: AWS Client VPN.
AWS Site-to-Site VPN.
Amazon WorkSpaces.
AWS Verified Access.
questions.explanation: Verified Access evaluates each request against identity (IAM Identity Center or OIDC) and device posture policies without a VPN. Client VPN and Site-to-Site VPN provide network-level access. WorkSpaces is virtual desktops.

questions.question: A developer accidentally committed AWS access keys to a public repository. What should be done FIRST?
options: Rewrite the Git history with a force push to remove the commit, then keep using the same keys because they are no longer publicly visible in the repository.
Deactivate/delete the exposed access keys immediately, then review CloudTrail for unauthorized activity and rotate to role-based credentials.
Enable GuardDuty and wait for a finding.
Change the IAM user console password.
questions.explanation: Revoking the exposed key stops misuse; then investigate CloudTrail and move to temporary credentials. Removing the commit does not revoke keys already scraped. Waiting for findings delays containment. Console passwords are separate from access keys.

questions.question: A healthcare company must investigate a GuardDuty finding showing unusual API calls from an IAM role, including visualizing related entities and behavior over time. Which service is BEST suited?
options: Amazon Macie.
Amazon Detective.
AWS Config timeline.
Amazon Inspector.
questions.explanation: Detective builds behavior graphs from CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, EKS audit logs, and GuardDuty findings to investigate root cause. Macie is data classification. Config shows resource configuration history. Inspector finds vulnerabilities.

questions.question: A company stores database credentials that must be accessible to a Lambda function with low latency and caching. Which is the recommended approach?
options: Store the secret in Secrets Manager and use the AWS Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension to cache it.
Store the password in plaintext Lambda environment variables so it is available instantly without extra API calls.
Hard-code it in the deployment package.
Store it in an S3 object with public access.
questions.explanation: Secrets Manager plus the extension provides secure retrieval with local caching, reducing latency and API calls. Plaintext environment variables and hard-coding expose secrets. Public S3 is insecure.

questions.question: A company requires that no S3 bucket in any account in the organization can ever be made public, and that the control cannot be changed by account admins. What is the MOST effective approach?
options: Enable S3 Block Public Access at the account level (or organization level policy) and use an SCP denying s3:PutAccountPublicAccessBlock changes.
Use an AWS Config managed rule to detect public buckets daily and send findings to the security team through SNS for manual remediation within 24 hours.
Train developers.
Enable Macie in every account.
questions.explanation: Account/org-level Block Public Access overrides bucket settings; an SCP prevents admins from disabling it. Config detects after exposure. Training is not a control. Macie finds sensitive data but does not block public access.

questions.question: A team needs to connect securely to EC2 instances in private subnets without opening SSH ports or managing bastion hosts. What should be used?
options: AWS Systems Manager Session Manager.
A hardened bastion host in a public subnet.
Opening port 22 to 0.0.0.0/0.
EC2 Serial Console for all access.
questions.explanation: Session Manager provides audited shell access via the SSM agent with IAM control and no inbound ports. Bastions add attack surface. Opening SSH to the world is insecure. Serial Console is for troubleshooting boot issues.

questions.question: A company has a generative AI application on Bedrock and must prevent the model from returning PII and off-topic content, and must verify factual claims against a policy document. What should be configured?
options: IAM policies denying bedrock:InvokeModel.
AWS WAF on the Bedrock endpoint.
Amazon Macie scanning prompts.
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails with sensitive information filters, denied topics, content filters, and Automated Reasoning checks.
questions.explanation: Guardrails filter harmful content, block topics, redact PII, and Automated Reasoning checks (GA August 2025) use formal logic to validate responses against policies. IAM denies stop all use. WAF does not understand model output semantics. Macie scans S3 data, not live prompts.

questions.question: Which encryption option gives S3 the ability to use a KMS key while reducing KMS request costs for high-volume workloads?
options: SSE-C.
Client-side encryption with a new key per object.
SSE-KMS with a new customer managed key per object.
SSE-KMS with S3 Bucket Keys enabled.
questions.explanation: S3 Bucket Keys generate a bucket-level data key, reducing KMS calls by up to 99%. SSE-C requires customers to manage keys per request. Per-object keys increase cost and management.

questions.question: A company wants to restrict usage of AWS to only approved Regions across all accounts. What is the simplest preventive control?
options: IAM policies in each account.
AWS Budgets alerts per Region.
Tag policies.
An SCP that denies actions when aws:RequestedRegion is not in the approved list (exempting global services), or the Control Tower Region deny control.
questions.explanation: SCPs with aws:RequestedRegion are a standard preventive guardrail, and Control Tower provides a managed Region deny control. Per-account IAM is hard to enforce. Budgets alert but do not prevent. Tag policies govern tags.

questions.question: A fintech company requires FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated, single-tenant HSMs that it fully controls for payment key operations. Which service should be used?
options: AWS KMS with customer managed keys, which are stored in FIPS-validated HSMs.
AWS CloudHSM (or AWS Payment Cryptography for payment-specific operations).
AWS Secrets Manager.
ACM Private CA only.
questions.explanation: CloudHSM provides dedicated, customer-controlled HSMs validated at FIPS 140-3 Level 3. KMS is multi-tenant (its HSMs are also FIPS validated, but keys are managed by the service). Secrets Manager stores secrets. Private CA issues certificates.

questions.question: An application running on EKS pods needs AWS permissions scoped per Kubernetes service account. Which feature should be used?
options: EKS Pod Identity (or IAM Roles for Service Accounts).
Attach an admin role to the worker node instance profile.
Store access keys in Kubernetes secrets.
Use the root user credentials.
questions.explanation: Pod Identity and IRSA give each service account a distinct IAM role with temporary credentials. Node roles give every pod the same permissions. Stored keys are long-term. Root credentials must never be used.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the AWS shared responsibility model for Amazon RDS?
options: The customer patches the RDS host OS.
AWS is responsible for customer data classification.
AWS manages the underlying infrastructure, OS, and database software patching; the customer manages network access, IAM, encryption choices, and database users.
The customer manages the physical data center security.
questions.explanation: For managed services like RDS, AWS takes on OS and engine patching and infrastructure; customers own configuration, access control, and data. Customers do not patch RDS hosts or secure data centers. Data classification is the customer responsibility.

questions.question: A company has AI agents deployed on Bedrock AgentCore that call internal tools through AgentCore Gateway. Security requires deterministic enforcement of which tools and parameters each agent can use, outside of the agent code. What should be configured?
options: A system prompt telling the agent which tools not to call.
A CloudWatch alarm on tool invocation counts.
AgentCore Policy, which intercepts Gateway tool calls and evaluates fine-grained policies before execution, combined with AgentCore Identity for credentials.
Bedrock model invocation logging only.
questions.explanation: AgentCore Policy (announced re:Invent 2025) enforces boundaries on agent actions deterministically at the Gateway, independent of model behavior; Identity manages the agent credentials. Prompts are not a security control. Alarms and logging are detective, not preventive.

questions.question: A company must meet a requirement to keep S3 objects immutable for 5 years for compliance, such that not even the root user can delete them. Which feature should be enabled?
options: S3 Object Lock in governance mode with a 5-year default retention.
S3 Versioning only.
An S3 Lifecycle expiration rule.
S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a 5-year retention period.
questions.explanation: Compliance mode prevents anyone, including root, from deleting or shortening retention. Governance mode can be bypassed with special permissions. Versioning allows deleting versions. Lifecycle rules delete objects.

questions.question: An application needs to encrypt data client-side before sending it to DynamoDB, with per-attribute encryption and signing. Which approach should be used?
options: DynamoDB default encryption at rest with an AWS owned key.
The AWS Database Encryption SDK with KMS keys.
TLS 1.3 only.
SSE-S3.
questions.explanation: The Database Encryption SDK provides client-side, attribute-level encryption and signing for DynamoDB. Default encryption protects at rest on the server side. TLS protects in transit. SSE-S3 is for S3.

questions.question: A company with many accounts wants to centrally manage WAF rules, Shield Advanced protections, and security group policies across the organization, automatically applying them to new resources. Which service should be used?
options: AWS Firewall Manager with a delegated administrator in Organizations.
AWS Config aggregators and conformance packs in a delegated administrator account.
AWS Control Tower account factory only.
Manual WAF configuration per account.
questions.explanation: Firewall Manager centrally deploys and enforces WAF, Shield Advanced, security group, Network Firewall, and DNS Firewall policies across accounts, including new resources. Config aggregators only report. Account factory vends accounts. Manual configuration does not scale.

questions.question: An EC2-hosted application needs to prevent SSRF attacks from stealing instance role credentials via the metadata service. What should be enforced?
options: Require IMDSv2 (session tokens) and set the hop limit appropriately.
Disable the instance role.
Use IMDSv1 only.
Open port 80 on the security group so the metadata service can be reached.
questions.explanation: IMDSv2 requires a PUT-obtained session token, mitigating most SSRF credential theft; hop limit 1 blocks forwarding from containers. Removing the role breaks the app. IMDSv1 is vulnerable. Opening ports is unrelated.

questions.question: A company wants a managed service to manage user identities and access for business applications such as Salesforce and Microsoft 365, along with AWS accounts, from one place. Which service is appropriate?
options: AWS IAM Identity Center.
Amazon Cognito identity pools.
IAM roles only.
AWS Directory Service AD Connector only.
questions.explanation: Identity Center provides SSO to AWS accounts and SAML 2.0 business applications with a central user portal. Cognito is for customer identities. IAM roles are per-account. AD Connector proxies to on-premises AD but does not provide the SSO portal by itself.

questions.question: An organization must prevent any principal in the org from accessing S3 buckets owned outside the organization (to stop data exfiltration), even with valid credentials. Which control is MOST effective?
options: An SCP denying S3 actions unless aws:ResourceOrgID equals the organization ID (with exceptions for required AWS-owned resources).
A bucket policy on each company bucket.
Macie findings on external buckets.
A NACL blocking S3 IP ranges.
questions.explanation: SCPs restrict identities in the org from accessing resources outside it, the identity-side data perimeter. Bucket policies only control your own buckets. Macie cannot see external buckets. NACL IP blocking would break legitimate S3 access and is brittle.

questions.question: A company wants to receive an alert when an IAM user signs in to the console without MFA. Which solution works with the LEAST effort?
options: Write a cron script on an EC2 instance that downloads and parses IAM credential reports every hour and emails the results.
Enable Amazon Inspector.
Use AWS Budgets alerts.
Create an EventBridge rule matching CloudTrail ConsoleLogin events with MFAUsed = No, targeting an SNS topic.
questions.explanation: EventBridge can match CloudTrail management events in near real time and notify via SNS. Credential reports are periodic and require scripting. Inspector and Budgets are unrelated.

questions.question: Which service should be used to issue private TLS certificates for internal microservices with automated renewal?
options: ACM public certificates.
AWS KMS asymmetric keys.
AWS Private Certificate Authority integrated with ACM.
Self-signed certificates generated with OpenSSL and stored in S3.
questions.explanation: AWS Private CA issues private certificates, and ACM can manage and renew them for integrated services. Public certificates are for public domains. KMS asymmetric keys are not certificates. Self-signed certs are unmanaged.

questions.question: A company runs agentic AI applications and wants AI-powered design security reviews, code analysis, and on-demand contextual penetration testing of its applications. Which recently launched AWS service addresses this?
options: AWS Security Agent.
Amazon Inspector Classic.
AWS Trusted Advisor.
AWS Artifact.
questions.explanation: AWS Security Agent (preview at re:Invent 2025, with STRIDE threat modeling and PR scanning added in 2026) performs design reviews, code analysis, and contextual penetration testing. Inspector Classic is retired. Trusted Advisor gives best-practice checks. Artifact provides compliance documents.

questions.question: A company wants to keep an audit trail of who accessed specific S3 objects (GetObject calls). What must be enabled?
options: CloudTrail management events only, delivered to a CloudTrail organization trail.
VPC Flow Logs.
AWS Config recording.
CloudTrail data events for the S3 bucket (or S3 server access logging).
questions.explanation: Object-level API calls are data events, which are not logged by default; server access logs are an alternative. Management events cover control-plane actions. Flow Logs show IP traffic. Config tracks configuration.

questions.question: A company wants to ensure data in transit between clients and an Application Load Balancer uses only modern TLS versions. What should be configured?
options: An HTTPS listener with an ACM certificate and a security policy that allows only TLS 1.2/1.3 (for example a TLS 1.3 policy, optionally with post-quantum key exchange).
A security group allowing only port 443.
Enable S3 default encryption.
Enable KMS automatic key rotation.
questions.explanation: ALB security policies define allowed TLS protocols and ciphers; ACM provides the certificate. Security groups control ports, not TLS versions. S3 encryption and KMS rotation concern data at rest.

questions.question: A company runs workloads in 150 accounts and wants to enforce that no one can create S3 buckets or KMS keys whose resource policies allow principals outside the organization, as a preventive control applied to resources rather than identities. What should be used?
options: Service control policies only, which restrict identities in the org.
IAM Access Analyzer archive rules.
Resource control policies (RCPs) in AWS Organizations, which set maximum permissions on resources such as S3 buckets and KMS keys regardless of their resource policies.
AWS Config rules with notifications.
questions.explanation: RCPs (launched November 2024) centrally restrict what external principals can do with your resources, complementing SCPs, which limit your own identities. Access Analyzer and Config detect but do not prevent. SCPs alone cannot stop external principals from using a permissive resource policy.

questions.question: A company runs a steady-state fleet of EC2 instances across several instance families and Regions, and also uses Fargate and Lambda. It wants the largest discount flexibility without committing to specific instance families. What should it purchase?
options: Compute Savings Plans.
EC2 Instance Savings Plans.
Standard Reserved Instances for each instance type.
Spot Instances for all workloads.
questions.explanation: Compute Savings Plans (up to 66% off) apply across instance family, size, Region, OS, tenancy, and also to Fargate and Lambda. EC2 Instance Savings Plans (up to 72%) lock to a family in a Region. Standard RIs are least flexible. Spot is not appropriate for steady-state critical workloads.

questions.question: Objects in an S3 bucket have unpredictable access patterns; some are read daily and others not for months. The team wants to minimize storage cost without managing lifecycle rules. Which storage class should be used?
options: S3 Standard.
S3 Intelligent-Tiering.
S3 One Zone-IA.
S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
questions.explanation: Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between access tiers based on usage with no retrieval fees, for a small monitoring fee per object. Standard does not optimize. One Zone-IA reduces resilience and charges retrieval fees. Deep Archive has 12–48 hour retrievals.

questions.question: Compliance requires keeping logs for 7 years. They are rarely accessed and retrieval within 48 hours is acceptable. What is the MOST cost-effective storage?
options: S3 Standard-IA.
S3 Glacier Deep Archive via a lifecycle rule.
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval.
EBS cold HDD (sc1) volumes.
questions.explanation: Deep Archive is the lowest-cost S3 storage class, with standard retrieval within 12 hours and bulk within 48 hours (180-day minimum). Standard-IA and Glacier Instant Retrieval cost more for storage. sc1 volumes are more expensive and not durable archive storage.

questions.question: A development environment of EC2 instances runs 24/7 but is only used during business hours. What reduces cost with LEAST effort?
options: Purchase 3-year All Upfront Reserved Instances for the fleet to get the deepest possible discount on the 24/7 usage.
Stop the instances outside business hours with AWS Instance Scheduler or an EventBridge Scheduler/SSM schedule.
Move to Dedicated Hosts.
Use larger instances so developers finish work faster and the environment needs fewer total instance hours.
questions.explanation: Stopping instances nights and weekends cuts compute cost by roughly 65–70%. RIs discount 24/7 usage you do not need. Dedicated Hosts cost more. Larger instances increase hourly cost.

questions.question: A company runs Aurora, RDS for PostgreSQL, ElastiCache, and DynamoDB, and plans to migrate some RDS workloads to Aurora and move Regions over the next year. Which commitment-based discount provides savings with this flexibility?
options: RDS Reserved Instances for each current instance, exchanged for new reservations whenever engines or Regions change.
Compute Savings Plans, which apply automatically across instance families, Regions, and managed databases.
EC2 Instance Savings Plans.
Database Savings Plans (1-year), which apply across engines, instance families, deployment options, and Regions.
questions.explanation: Database Savings Plans (launched December 2025) give up to 35% savings and apply automatically across Aurora, RDS, DynamoDB, ElastiCache, DocumentDB, Neptune, Keyspaces, Timestream, DMS, and later OpenSearch, even when changing engines or Regions. RDS RIs are tied to engine/family/Region. Compute and EC2 Savings Plans do not cover managed databases.

questions.question: A company wants to be alerted when its monthly AWS spend is forecasted to exceed $50,000. Which service should be used?
options: AWS Budgets with a forecasted cost alert.
AWS Cost Explorer reports reviewed monthly.
Amazon CloudWatch billing metric with a 1-minute period.
AWS Trusted Advisor.
questions.explanation: AWS Budgets supports actual and forecasted cost alerts and budget actions. Cost Explorer is for analysis, not alerting. The CloudWatch billing metric alerts on actual charges, not forecasts. Trusted Advisor provides recommendations.

questions.question: An application has a NAT gateway processing terabytes per month, mostly traffic to S3 and DynamoDB. How can data processing charges be reduced?
options: Create gateway VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB so that traffic bypasses the NAT gateway for free.
Replace the NAT gateway with an internet gateway for private subnets.
Add a second NAT gateway so the data processing charges are split across two gateways.
Use interface VPC endpoints for S3 in every AZ so the traffic stays private and no longer passes through the NAT gateway.
questions.explanation: Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are free and remove NAT data processing charges for that traffic. Private subnets cannot use an IGW directly. Another NAT gateway adds cost. Interface endpoints for S3 have hourly and per-GB charges, useful for on-premises access but costlier here.

questions.question: A fault-tolerant, stateless batch workload can run on any of several instance types and tolerate interruptions. What is the MOST cost-effective compute option?
options: On-Demand Instances in an Auto Scaling group that scales to zero when the batch queue is empty.
Spot Instances via an ASG or EC2 Fleet with multiple instance types and the price-capacity-optimized strategy.
3-year All Upfront Reserved Instances, which give the largest discount for any workload that runs regularly.
Dedicated Instances.
questions.explanation: Spot provides up to 90% discount for interruptible workloads; diversification reduces interruptions. On-Demand costs more. RIs require long commitments for possibly intermittent jobs. Dedicated Instances are more expensive.

questions.question: A company notices that data transfer costs between EC2 instances in different AZs are high for a chatty microservices application. What change reduces cost while keeping resilience?
options: Keep calls within the same AZ where possible (AZ-aware/topology-aware routing) while still deploying across multiple AZs.
Move all services into a single AZ permanently and rely on Auto Scaling to replace failed instances.
Route inter-service traffic through a NAT gateway so that it stays within the VPC and is not charged per GB.
Split the application into multiple VPCs peered together, because traffic over VPC peering connections is not billed for data transfer.
questions.explanation: Cross-AZ data transfer is charged per GB in each direction; AZ-affinity routing reduces it while retaining multi-AZ deployment for failover. A single AZ sacrifices resilience. NAT gateways add processing charges. Peering does not remove cross-AZ charges.

questions.question: Which tool shows historical cost and usage with filtering by service, account, and tags, plus 12-month forecasts?
options: AWS Budgets.
AWS Cost Explorer.
AWS Pricing Calculator.
AWS Config.
questions.explanation: Cost Explorer visualizes historical cost and usage (13 months by default) and forecasts future spend. Budgets tracks thresholds. Pricing Calculator estimates future architectures. Config tracks resource configuration.

questions.question: A team runs an RDS for MySQL instance for a test database used a few hours per week, with unpredictable timing. Which option minimizes cost?
options: A provisioned db.r7g.4xlarge with a Reserved Instance to get the lowest hourly rate for the database.
Aurora Serverless v2 (MySQL-compatible), which scales down to 0 ACUs with auto-pause when idle.
RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster.
Amazon Redshift provisioned cluster.
questions.explanation: Aurora Serverless v2 scales in fine-grained increments and supports scaling to zero with auto-pause, so idle time costs only storage. A large RI charges 24/7. Multi-AZ clusters triple instance cost. Redshift is a warehouse.

questions.question: A company pays for many unattached EBS volumes and old snapshots. Which approach helps find and clean them up?
options: Enable EBS encryption by default in each Region so unattached volumes and old snapshots are no longer billed at the full per-GB rate.
Move EBS volumes to instance store, which is included in the instance price and has no per-GB charge.
Use Trusted Advisor, Cost Optimization Hub, and Compute Optimizer idle findings, then delete or archive unneeded resources.
Enable detailed monitoring so CloudWatch automatically deletes volumes that have been unattached for 30 days.
questions.explanation: Trusted Advisor and Cost Optimization Hub flag underutilized/unattached volumes; Compute Optimizer identifies idle resources; snapshot archive reduces snapshot costs by up to 75%. Encryption and monitoring do not reduce cost. Instance store is not a replacement for persistent volumes.

questions.question: A startup serves 40 TB/month of static content through CloudFront with occasional viral spikes and DDoS attempts, and wants predictable monthly bills including WAF and DNS. Which option fits BEST?
options: A CloudFront flat-rate pricing plan (for example Business or Premium tier) that bundles CDN, WAF, DDoS protection, Route 53 DNS, and S3 credits with no overage charges.
Pay-as-you-go CloudFront with a CloudWatch billing alarm.
CloudFront Security Savings Bundle only.
Serve directly from S3 to avoid CloudFront costs.
questions.explanation: Flat-rate plans (November 2025) charge a fixed monthly price with usage allowances (Pro/Business/Premium include 50 TB transfer) and no overages; blocked attacks do not count. Pay-as-you-go varies with spikes. The savings bundle is a commitment discount, not a fixed price. Serving from S3 costs more for egress and loses edge protection.

questions.question: An S3 bucket contains objects that are accessed frequently for 30 days, rarely for the next 60 days, and never after 1 year. Which lifecycle configuration is MOST cost-effective?
options: Transition to Standard-IA after 30 days, to Glacier Flexible Retrieval (or Deep Archive) after 90 days, and expire at 365 days.
Keep all objects in S3 Standard indefinitely.
Transition everything to S3 Glacier Deep Archive on day 1 to get the lowest possible storage price from the start.
Transition all objects to S3 One Zone-IA on day 1 to cut storage costs immediately, and never expire them in case they are needed later.
questions.explanation: Lifecycle transitions match storage class to access patterns and expiration removes unneeded data. Keeping everything in Standard wastes money. Archiving on day 1 breaks frequent access. One Zone-IA on day 1 adds retrieval fees during frequent access and never deletes.

questions.question: A Lambda-based API handles 5 million requests per day with an average duration of 800 ms at 2 GB memory. What change often reduces cost with no code change?
options: Increase the timeout to 15 minutes so that fewer invocations fail and have to be retried and billed again.
Enable provisioned concurrency for all of the traffic, since provisioned environments are billed at a lower GB-second rate than on-demand.
Switch the function to arm64 (Graviton), which has a lower GB-second price, and right-size memory with Lambda Power Tuning.
Put the function in a VPC.
questions.explanation: arm64 Lambda is up to 20% cheaper per GB-second with often better performance; tuning memory finds the best cost/speed point. Timeouts do not reduce cost. Provisioned concurrency adds cost unless utilization is high. VPC placement does not reduce cost.

questions.question: A company runs Lambda functions with steady, high-volume traffic 24/7 and wants to use EC2 pricing models such as Savings Plans and specific instance types without managing servers. What recent option addresses this?
options: Lambda provisioned concurrency on x86, covered by a Compute Savings Plan for the steady baseline.
AWS Lambda Managed Instances, which run functions on EC2 capacity providers at EC2 pricing plus a management fee.
Migrate the functions to containers on an EC2 Auto Scaling group and take over OS patching, scaling, and runtime management yourself.
Use Lambda@Edge.
questions.explanation: Lambda Managed Instances (re:Invent 2025) keep the Lambda programming model while billing EC2 instance price (eligible for Savings Plans/RIs) plus a 15% management fee and request charges; no per-duration charge and multiple concurrent requests per environment. Provisioned concurrency still bills per GB-second. Self-managed EC2 adds ops. Lambda@Edge is for CloudFront.

questions.question: An organization with 50 accounts wants consolidated billing and to share Reserved Instance and Savings Plans discounts across accounts. What should be used?
options: AWS Organizations consolidated billing (discount sharing enabled).
Separate payment methods per account.
AWS Control Tower account factory only.
IAM Identity Center.
questions.explanation: Consolidated billing in Organizations aggregates usage for volume discounts and shares RI/Savings Plans benefits across accounts. Separate payments lose sharing. Account factory and Identity Center do not handle billing.

questions.question: A company wants to allocate costs to business units. Which practice enables this in Cost Explorer and the Cost and Usage Report?
options: Use a separate Region per business unit.
Enable CloudTrail.
Use different instance types per business unit and map spend back using the instance-type breakdown in Cost Explorer.
Apply a consistent tagging strategy and activate cost allocation tags (optionally use AWS Cost Categories).
questions.explanation: Activated cost allocation tags and cost categories group spend by business dimension. Regions, CloudTrail, and instance types do not provide allocation.

questions.question: A data platform stores 2 PB in S3 Standard and queries a small fraction regularly. An analysis shows 70% of objects have not been accessed for 180 days, but some may be needed within milliseconds. Which option reduces cost the MOST while preserving millisecond access?
options: Move all cold data to S3 Glacier Deep Archive, the lowest-cost storage class, and restore on demand.
Move cold data to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval (or Intelligent-Tiering Archive Instant Access).
Keep the data in S3 Standard and enable Requester Pays so consuming teams pay for the storage they use.
Move data to EBS sc1 volumes.
questions.explanation: Glacier Instant Retrieval provides millisecond retrieval at much lower storage cost for data accessed about once per quarter; Intelligent-Tiering Archive Instant Access offers similar economics automatically. Deep Archive needs hours to restore. Requester Pays shifts request costs, not storage. EBS is more expensive.

questions.question: Which EC2 purchasing option allows reserving capacity in a specific AZ for any duration without a long-term commitment?
options: Spot blocks.
On-Demand Capacity Reservations.
Standard Reserved Instances with Regional scope.
Savings Plans.
questions.explanation: On-Demand Capacity Reservations reserve capacity in an AZ and can be created or cancelled anytime (billed at On-Demand rates, discountable with Savings Plans). Spot blocks are discontinued. Regional RIs do not reserve capacity. Savings Plans provide discounts, not capacity.

questions.question: A company runs a large Amazon DynamoDB table with predictable steady traffic. How can it reduce throughput costs?
options: Use on-demand capacity mode for all tables, since it scales instantly and bills only for requests made.
Enable global tables so that read and write capacity is spread across multiple Regions at a lower rate.
Use provisioned capacity with auto scaling plus reserved capacity (or Database Savings Plans).
Increase item size.
questions.explanation: For steady, predictable workloads, provisioned capacity with reserved capacity is cheaper than on-demand. Global tables add replicated write costs. Larger items consume more capacity.

questions.question: A company runs a large EKS cluster with mixed workloads and poor bin-packing, leading to many underutilized nodes. Which approach reduces compute cost MOST with low operational effort?
options: Increase the node group minimum size so pods are always scheduled on warm nodes without waiting.
Use only the largest instance type in the node group so more pods fit per node and fewer nodes are needed overall.
Disable Horizontal Pod Autoscaler.
Use Karpenter or EKS Auto Mode to consolidate and right-size nodes, with Spot and Graviton where possible.
questions.explanation: Karpenter/EKS Auto Mode consolidate workloads onto fewer, cheaper nodes and choose instance types dynamically, including Spot and Graviton. Larger minimums and a single big instance type waste capacity. Disabling HPA removes elasticity.

questions.question: Which AWS tool estimates the monthly cost of a proposed architecture before deployment?
options: AWS Cost Explorer.
AWS Budgets.
AWS Pricing Calculator.
AWS Compute Optimizer.
questions.explanation: Pricing Calculator models new or planned workloads. Cost Explorer analyzes actual historical costs. Budgets alerts on thresholds. Compute Optimizer recommends based on existing utilization.

questions.question: A company transfers 100 TB per month from EC2 to the internet for software downloads. How can it reduce data transfer out costs?
options: Move the EC2 instances to a different Availability Zone with lower internet data transfer rates and serve the downloads from there.
Serve downloads through CloudFront; transfer from AWS origins to CloudFront is free and CloudFront egress rates are lower.
Use a larger instance type with higher network bandwidth so downloads complete faster and cost less.
Enable S3 Requester Pays on the EC2 instances so the downloading customers pay for the data transfer.
questions.explanation: Origin fetches from AWS origins to CloudFront incur no data transfer charges, and caching reduces origin load. AZ and instance size do not change egress pricing. Requester Pays applies to S3 buckets, not EC2.

questions.question: A company uses a single large m5.24xlarge On-Demand instance for a Windows SQL Server license-included workload with low CPU utilization. Which change reduces cost the MOST?
options: Buy a 3-year All Upfront Reserved Instance for the same m5.24xlarge to lock in the maximum possible discount on the current size and SQL license.
Move the workload to a Dedicated Host of the same size so the license-included SQL Server charges are billed at a lower per-core rate.
Right-size with Compute Optimizer (including license recommendations), optimize CPUs, and adopt newer instances or RDS with a Savings Plan.
Add a second identical instance for HA.
questions.explanation: Right-sizing and optimizing vCPUs reduces both compute and per-core licensing; Compute Optimizer provides SQL Server licensing recommendations. Locking in an oversized instance wastes money. Dedicated Hosts only help with BYOL. Adding instances increases cost.

questions.question: An application stores thumbnails that can be regenerated from originals if lost. Which S3 storage class is cheapest for infrequently accessed thumbnails?
options: S3 Standard.
S3 Standard-IA.
S3 One Zone-IA.
S3 Express One Zone.
questions.explanation: One Zone-IA is about 20% cheaper than Standard-IA and appropriate for re-creatable, infrequently accessed data. Standard and Standard-IA cost more. Express One Zone is high-performance, higher-priced storage for low-latency access.

questions.question: A company wants to automatically stop an EC2 instance if a project exceeds its monthly budget. What should be configured?
options: A CloudTrail trail.
An AWS Budgets action that applies an IAM/SCP policy or stops targeted EC2/RDS instances at the threshold.
An AWS Config rule that evaluates project spend and marks instances noncompliant over budget.
Cost Explorer saved reports scheduled to run daily, with the instance stopped automatically when the report shows an overspend.
questions.explanation: Budgets actions can automatically apply policies or stop EC2/RDS instances. CloudTrail logs API calls. Config evaluates configurations. Cost Explorer reports do not act.

questions.question: A media company stores 500 TB on EFS Standard, but analysis shows 80% of files are not accessed after 30 days. What reduces cost with LEAST effort?
options: Migrate the files to EBS volumes.
Switch to provisioned throughput mode, which lowers the per-GB storage price for large file systems.
Enable EFS lifecycle management to move files to Infrequent Access and Archive classes (and back on access).
Copy the files to S3 nightly with a script and delete them from EFS, recreating them when users request them.
questions.explanation: EFS lifecycle policies transition cold files to IA and Archive classes at much lower cost, and can move them back on access. EBS is not shared storage. Provisioned throughput adds cost. Custom copy scripts add operational burden and break file semantics.

questions.question: Which statement about Savings Plans is correct?
options: Savings Plans give lower prices in exchange for a consistent $/hour usage commitment for 1 or 3 years.
Savings Plans reserve EC2 capacity in a specific AZ in addition to providing a discounted rate.
Savings Plans can be cancelled at any time without cost if your usage drops below the commitment level.
Savings Plans apply only to EC2 in one Region.
questions.explanation: Savings Plans are an hourly spend commitment over 1 or 3 years. They do not reserve capacity (use Capacity Reservations), cannot be cancelled freely, and Compute Savings Plans apply across Regions and to Fargate and Lambda.

questions.question: A company has many small, idle load balancers and Elastic IPs in development accounts. Which service provides a consolidated view of cost optimization recommendations across accounts?
options: AWS Cost Optimization Hub (in the Billing and Cost Management console), alongside Trusted Advisor.
Amazon Inspector.
AWS Artifact.
AWS CloudShell.
questions.explanation: Cost Optimization Hub aggregates and prioritizes recommendations such as idle resources, rightsizing, and commitments across the organization. Inspector, Artifact, and CloudShell are not cost tools.

questions.question: A company moves an on-premises Hadoop cluster to AWS. Jobs run for 4 hours nightly on 200 nodes. Which architecture minimizes cost?
options: A persistent EMR cluster with HDFS on EBS running 24/7 so data stays local to compute.
Keep data in S3 and run transient EMR clusters (or EMR Serverless) nightly with Spot task nodes.
EC2 On-Demand instances with Hadoop installed manually, always on, covered by Reserved Instances.
Redshift provisioned cluster with 200 nodes.
questions.explanation: Decoupling storage (S3) from compute allows transient clusters that exist only during jobs, and Spot task nodes cut costs further. Persistent clusters pay for 20 idle hours. Manual EC2 adds ops and idle cost. Redshift is a different engine and overprovisioned.

questions.question: A developer wants to be notified when CloudWatch Logs ingestion costs spike due to verbose debug logging. What is a quick approach?
options: Enable VPC Flow Logs.
Create an AWS Budgets cost budget filtered to CloudWatch (or Cost Anomaly Detection monitor) with alerts.
Disable CloudTrail.
Use AWS X-Ray sampling.
questions.explanation: Budgets filtered by service or Cost Anomaly Detection alert on unexpected spend. Flow Logs add cost. Disabling CloudTrail harms security. X-Ray sampling affects traces, not log ingestion.

questions.question: A company is choosing between gp2 and gp3 for 500 EBS volumes. What is the typical cost benefit of gp3?
options: gp3 is more expensive but faster.
gp3 only supports magnetic storage.
gp3 is about 20% cheaper per GB than gp2 and has a 3,000 IOPS / 125 MiB/s baseline at any size.
gp2 allows provisioning IOPS independently of size, while gp3 ties IOPS to the volume size in GiB.
questions.explanation: gp3 offers lower per-GB pricing with baseline performance decoupled from size. gp2 IOPS scale with size (3 IOPS/GB). gp3 is SSD.

questions.question: A company needs a cost-effective vector store for 1 billion embeddings used for infrequent RAG queries where 100-ms latency is acceptable. Which option minimizes cost?
options: An always-on OpenSearch Service cluster with memory-optimized data nodes sized to hold all 1 billion vectors in RAM.
Amazon S3 Vectors (optionally with Bedrock Knowledge Bases), which AWS says cuts vector cost by up to 90%.
Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector on the largest instance class, with HNSW indexes kept in memory.
ElastiCache for Valkey with vector search, keeping all 1 billion embeddings in memory for fast queries.
questions.explanation: S3 Vectors (GA December 2025) stores up to 2 billion vectors per index with ~100 ms query latency at far lower cost for infrequent queries. In-memory OpenSearch, pgvector on large instances, or ElastiCache vector search are optimized for low latency/high QPS at much higher cost.

questions.question: A team runs Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints that sit idle overnight. What reduces cost for this intermittent inference traffic?
options: Add more instances to the endpoint.
Use SageMaker Serverless Inference or asynchronous inference with scale-to-zero, or Bedrock on-demand if a foundation model fits.
Use a larger GPU instance.
Enable Multi-AZ on the endpoint.
questions.explanation: Serverless inference and async endpoints scale to zero when idle; Bedrock charges per token. Adding or enlarging instances increases idle cost. Multi-AZ adds instances.

questions.question: A company wants to reduce costs for Amazon Bedrock inference on a batch of 1 million documents that do not need real-time responses. What should they use?
options: Provisioned Throughput with a 6-month commitment.
Bedrock batch inference, which is priced at a discount compared with on-demand.
Invoke the model on-demand synchronously in a tight loop from a fleet of Lambda functions.
Deploy the model to EC2 with GPUs 24/7.
questions.explanation: Batch inference processes large offline jobs at roughly 50% lower price than on-demand for supported models. Provisioned Throughput suits steady high-volume real-time needs. Synchronous loops pay full price and risk throttling. Self-hosting on GPUs 24/7 adds cost and ops.

questions.question: A company has variable workloads across EC2, Fargate, and Lambda with a stable baseline around $40/hour and peaks up to $120/hour. How should it size a Savings Plan commitment?
options: Commit near the steady baseline (about $40/hour) using Savings Plans recommendations, and cover peaks with On-Demand/Spot.
Commit to $120/hour to cover the peaks, since unused commitment rolls over to the following hour.
Commit to the average of peak and baseline ($80/hour) so that most hours of usage are covered by the discounted Savings Plans rate.
Avoid Savings Plans entirely.
questions.explanation: Savings Plans charge the committed amount every hour whether used or not, so committing to the baseline maximizes utilization. Committing to peaks leads to paying for unused commitment. No commitment forgoes significant savings.

questions.question: Which S3 feature reduces cost for requests where the requester, rather than the bucket owner, should pay for data transfer and requests?
options: S3 Transfer Acceleration.
Requester Pays buckets.
S3 Object Lock.
S3 Inventory.
questions.explanation: Requester Pays shifts request and download charges to the requester (who must be authenticated). Transfer Acceleration adds cost. Object Lock and Inventory are unrelated to who pays.

questions.question: A web application on EC2 has CPU utilization averaging 5% on m5.2xlarge instances. What is the first cost optimization step?
options: Purchase Reserved Instances for the current size first to lock in savings, then review utilization and sizing next year.
Right-size to a smaller or burstable instance (e.g., Graviton m7g/t4g) based on Compute Optimizer findings.
Enable Enhanced Networking so the instances process requests faster and can be stopped more often.
Move to a Dedicated Host.
questions.explanation: Right-sizing before committing avoids locking in waste. RIs for oversized instances lock in cost. Enhanced networking does not reduce cost. Dedicated Hosts are more expensive.

questions.question: A company runs an analytics platform on a provisioned Redshift RA3 cluster that is busy 9am-6pm on weekdays and nearly idle otherwise. Which change MOST reduces cost while keeping performance during business hours?
options: Migrate to Redshift Serverless (paying per RPU-second with automatic pause when idle), or pause/resume the provisioned cluster on a schedule.
Purchase 3-year All Upfront Reserved Nodes for the current cluster size to lock in the largest discount on all 24 hours of capacity.
Add concurrency scaling clusters for off-hours.
Convert all tables to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
questions.explanation: Serverless bills only for compute used, and scheduled pause/resume stops compute billing when idle; RA3 managed storage keeps data available. Reserved Nodes discount 24/7 capacity that is mostly idle. Concurrency scaling adds capacity rather than removing it. Deep Archive data cannot be queried directly.

questions.question: A team wants to deploy identical infrastructure to dev, test, and prod using code, with change previews before updates. Which approach is BEST?
options: Create resources manually in the console for each environment and document every step in a shared runbook so engineers can repeat them consistently.
Define infrastructure in AWS CloudFormation (or CDK) templates with parameters per environment and use change sets before updates.
Use AWS Config to replicate resources.
Copy AMIs between accounts.
questions.explanation: IaC with change sets provides repeatable deployments and previews of changes. Manual steps drift. Config records configuration, it does not deploy. AMIs cover instances only.

questions.question: An operations team needs to patch hundreds of EC2 instances on a schedule with compliance reporting. Which service should be used?
options: AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager with maintenance windows (or Quick Setup patch policies).
AWS Config rules with remediation actions only, triggered when an instance reports missing patches.
Amazon Inspector.
EC2 user data scripts.
questions.explanation: Patch Manager applies patch baselines on schedules across fleets and reports compliance. Config can trigger remediation but is not a patching engine. Inspector finds vulnerabilities but does not patch. User data runs only at launch.

questions.question: A developer needs to trace requests through API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB to find the slowest component. Which service provides this?
options: AWS CloudTrail data events for Lambda invocations and DynamoDB item-level calls.
AWS X-Ray (or CloudWatch Application Signals built on OpenTelemetry).
VPC Flow Logs.
AWS Config.
questions.explanation: X-Ray and Application Signals provide distributed tracing with service maps and latency breakdowns. CloudTrail logs API management calls. Flow Logs record network flows. Config tracks resource configuration.

questions.question: A company wants CloudWatch alarms to avoid paging on-call engineers for transient single-metric blips and only alert when both high latency and high error rate occur together. What should be used?
options: Two separate CloudWatch alarms, one for latency and one for error rate, each paging on-call directly.
A CloudWatch composite alarm combining the latency and error-rate alarms with AND logic.
A metric math expression with a 1-second period.
AWS Health Dashboard.
questions.explanation: Composite alarms reduce noise by alerting only when a rule over multiple alarms is met. Separate alarms page on each blip. Metric math can combine but a composite alarm is the purpose-built way to combine alarm states. Health Dashboard reports AWS service events.

questions.question: An application writes logs to CloudWatch Logs. The team wants to query logs ad hoc to find the top error messages over the last hour. What should they use?
options: CloudTrail Lake SQL queries.
Amazon Athena on EBS.
CloudWatch Logs Insights.
AWS X-Ray.
questions.explanation: Logs Insights provides an interactive query language over CloudWatch Logs. CloudTrail Lake queries API events. Athena queries S3, not EBS. X-Ray is tracing.

questions.question: An enterprise wants an on-call assistant that investigates incidents autonomously by correlating CloudWatch telemetry, deployments, and code changes to suggest root causes and mitigations. Which AWS service targets this?
options: AWS DevOps Agent (generally available since March 2026).
AWS Trusted Advisor operational excellence and fault tolerance checks.
AWS Health Aware.
Amazon Inspector.
questions.explanation: AWS DevOps Agent acts as an autonomous on-call engineer, analyzing observability data and code/deployment history to identify root causes and coordinate response. Trusted Advisor gives best-practice checks. Health events report AWS-side issues. Inspector scans vulnerabilities.
